teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an operations manager saying, “We need a new order system.” That names a possible solution, but it leaves the underlying problem unclear. For this example, suppose dispatch staff at the North branch cannot find the latest delivery instructions, and repeated clarification calls delay dispatch. Those details let you frame a problem without deciding what to buy.

teaching_blocks.title: Problem Definition and Scoping
teaching_blocks.content: Problem framing clarifies the problem rather than choosing a solution.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a concise problem statement identifying who is affected, what the problem is, why it matters, and where it occurs. State what work is included and what is excluded to make the scope boundary explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
A bounded statement could read: “North-branch dispatch staff cannot reliably find the latest delivery instructions when preparing an order, causing repeated clarification calls and delayed dispatch.” It identifies who is affected, what is wrong, why it matters, and where it occurs. The sentence does not promise that a new system is the right response.

Now write the boundary beside it: “Included: finding and communicating the latest delivery instructions during North-branch dispatch preparation. Excluded: changing delivery prices, replacing vehicles, or changing other branches' operations.” These are invented boundaries for this exercise, not general exclusions for every BA assignment. If a stakeholder asks to redesign vehicle purchasing, compare that request with the stated included and excluded work. The useful output is a problem statement and an explicit boundary, not a list of features disguised as a problem.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: “Implement an app” is not the same as clarifying the problem. Reword it around the affected people and difficulty before deciding on a solution. A concise problem statement also does not replace the included and excluded work: both need to be visible.

teaching_notes: Keep solution requirements and document templates for later; establish the problem and boundary first.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose dispatch staff describe delivery instructions as “hard to use.” You need to learn what happens during preparation, not persuade them that a particular replacement is desirable. Set the interview aim as understanding the expected outcome, current operating conditions, and constraints on accessing instructions.

teaching_blocks.title: Structured Interviews
teaching_blocks.content: A structured interview follows an interview script, unlike a semistructured interview’s flexibly ordered guide.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define what needs to be learned and prepare questions that address those aims. Ask concise, open-ended questions that let the participant describe their experience without suggesting the answer. Record the elicited needs in a shared requirements document with links to the supporting interview context. Probe vague answers with follow-up questions about concrete expected outcomes, operating conditions and constraints, and observable or measurable criteria showing that the requirement has been met.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Prepare a script with questions such as “Describe how you find the instructions for an order,” “What information do you need before dispatch?” and “What happens when that information is unclear?” A structured interview follows that script; a flexibly ordered guide would instead be semistructured. Keep each question concise and leave room for the participant’s own account.

When a participant says, “It should be quick,” ask what concrete outcome they expect, under which conditions, and what observable or measurable result would show that the need is met. For this hypothetical interview, they might specify finding the current instructions within 30 seconds during dispatch preparation. Record that elicited need in the shared requirements document and link it to the interview context, including the conditions discussed. The numerical threshold is example stakeholder input, not a universal requirement. The finished record should preserve both the stated need and the context that supports it, rather than only your summary of “make it faster.”

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Open-ended does not mean directionless: the questions still serve defined learning aims. Conversely, asking “Would a new mobile screen fix this?” suggests an answer instead of letting the participant describe their experience. A vague answer calls for concrete follow-up, not an invented requirement.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not turn this into workshop facilitation or survey design; teach script, open questions, probing, and contextual recording first.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine dispatch, sales, and customer-support representatives disagreeing about which delivery instructions must be available before dispatch. A workshop brings them together for goal-oriented activities and discussion. Define its outcome as a shared account of the information needed, with any unresolved questions recorded.

teaching_blocks.title: Facilitated Workshops
teaching_blocks.content: A workshop uses goal-oriented group activities and discussion to produce shared outcomes.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Build the agenda by defining goals, identifying questions needed to reach them, and choosing activities that answer those questions. Allocate time to each workshop segment and prepare the materials needed to capture discussion. Guide discussion toward the agenda goals and analyze and share the collected outputs after the workshop.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Build the agenda from that goal. Questions might include “What must dispatch know?” and “Which team supplies each piece of information?” Choose activities that address those questions, such as having participants describe an order and then discuss the required information together. In this hypothetical agenda, allocate ten minutes to the goal, twenty to the order exercise, twenty to discussion, and ten to consolidating outputs. Prepare a shared capture sheet before the session so contributed requirements and questions have a place to go.

During discussion, guide contributions back to the agenda’s questions. A lengthy discussion of vehicle purchasing does not answer the agreed information question, so return to the intended outcome. Afterward, analyze the captured material and share the resulting requirements and unresolved questions with participants. The workshop is not finished merely because its time has elapsed: the collected outputs still need analysis and sharing. The example timings and activity are choices for this situation, not a mandatory workshop format.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A workshop is not simply several people receiving the same presentation. Its activities and discussion are directed at shared outcomes. A detailed agenda helps only when its questions and activities actually support the agreed goals.

video_need.reason: A facilitated session demonstration can show how activities and discussion are guided toward a shared outcome; the text supplies the planning logic.

teaching_notes: Keep named workshop methodologies short; avoid implying one mandatory agenda sequence.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an order-service team wants to understand preferences across several branches. The research aim is to compare how important respondents consider finding delivery instructions quickly. A survey fits that attitudinal question better than a request for a detailed account of everything someone actually does during dispatch.

teaching_blocks.title: Surveys and Questionnaires
teaching_blocks.content: Surveys are best suited to collecting quantitative attitudinal data rather than detailed accounts of behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Include questions needed to answer the research aims rather than collecting information simply because it is easy to ask for. Write questions that respondents can answer accurately and avoid language that leads them toward a preferred answer.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
An example question could be “How important is access to the latest delivery instructions when preparing dispatch?” with clearly stated response options. Another could ask how satisfied the respondent is with current access. Keep questions tied to the stated research aim. Asking about unrelated office preferences would collect information without answering the requirements question.

Compare “How satisfied are you with the current instruction lookup?” with “How much do you love our improved lookup?” The second pushes toward a favorable answer. Also check whether respondents can accurately answer what is being asked: a person who does not prepare dispatch may not be able to describe that experience. In this exercise, the survey’s output is quantified attitudes and preferences about instruction access. It is not a reconstruction of the actual sequence of dispatch work. Maintain that distinction when explaining the results to stakeholders so the requirements discussion does not treat a preference score as a detailed behavioral account.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A large set of responses does not change the kind of evidence collected. Stated attitudes remain attitudes; they are not detailed observations of behavior. Easy-to-ask questions also do not belong automatically: each should serve the research aims.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce sampling statistics or claim surveys directly establish actual behavior.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine being given an old dispatch manual and a contract for an order-service change. The manual says a supervisor approves amended delivery instructions; the contract says the service must retain an instruction record. These are example statements from existing material, not requirements you have independently confirmed.

teaching_blocks.title: Document Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: Existing documentation is one channel for gathering requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Extract the requirements, assumptions, constraints, and open questions found in existing material and record them in one shared document with links to supporting context. Confirm the documented requirements with stakeholders before treating them as execution work.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Review the material systematically and record what each statement contributes. Put the approval requirement and record-retention constraint in the shared requirements document, linking each to the supporting manual or contract passage. If the manual assumes that only one branch processes an order, record that assumption too. If the contract does not identify who may amend instructions, record an open question rather than filling the gap with your own preference.

Then confirm the documented requirements with the relevant stakeholders before treating them as work to execute. For example, ask whether the supervisor approval rule is still intended and which scope it covers. A stakeholder might confirm it, request a change, or leave a question unresolved; preserve the resulting understanding in the shared record. The practical skill is extracting requirements, assumptions, constraints, and questions with their context intact. Merely copying paragraphs into a new file leaves the learner without a clear account of what has been found and what still needs confirmation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Existing text is an elicitation channel, not automatic confirmation that every old statement should be implemented now. Keep the supporting context and confirm requirements with stakeholders; do not silently turn an unresolved passage into an agreed requirement.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Avoid contractual or regulatory interpretation; use invented document statements only.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a dispatcher says, “I open the order and send it to the driver.” Observe the dispatcher doing the work in its actual context, then ask about the actions you saw. In this example, you observe the dispatcher open the order, consult a separate instruction sheet, call sales to clarify an address, and then send the order to the driver.

teaching_blocks.title: Observation Techniques
teaching_blocks.content: Observation examines what users do in their work context rather than relying solely on their account of what they do.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Observe the user perform work, then ask questions about what was observed. Record the tasks performed and analyze their sequence and subtasks to understand how the goal is achieved. Record the user’s stated process, compare it with the steps observed during actual work, and log discrepancies with notes of the observed actions that support them.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Record the performed tasks and their sequence. You can describe the goal as preparing an order for dispatch and identify subtasks such as finding instructions and resolving uncertainty. Ask questions about those observed steps: “What information were you checking on the separate sheet?” or “What made the clarification call necessary?” These questions follow the observation instead of replacing it with a guessed explanation.

Keep the stated process alongside the observed process. The statement omitted the separate-sheet lookup and clarification call; log that discrepancy with notes of the observed actions that support it. Do not change the observation record to make the two accounts agree. The comparison helps you understand how this work was actually performed in the observed situation. It does not establish that every dispatcher always follows the same sequence. The useful result is a supported account of tasks and discrepancies that can inform requirements, not a judgment about whether the participant gave a good interview answer.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Observation is more than asking someone what they normally do. It examines work as performed and then uses questions to understand what was seen. A difference between an account and observed steps should be documented with action notes, not replaced by speculation about motive.

video_need.reason: A work-context demonstration can make the contrast between a stated process and observed subtasks visible.

teaching_notes: Keep process notation for later; teach task records and stated-versus-observed comparison.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine stakeholders agreeing that dispatch staff need “a fast instruction lookup.” Agreement confirms an intended need, but the wording still leaves several questions: what counts as fast, under what conditions, and how will anyone determine whether the requirement has been met?

teaching_blocks.title: Requirements Validation and Verification
teaching_blocks.content: Validation with stakeholders confirms priorities and agreement about what will be delivered.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: For the requirements review, present the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions, then capture stakeholder agreement or requested changes. Distinguish validation of the intended business need with stakeholders from verification of the written requirements’ quality: stakeholder agreement does not by itself establish that the wording is unambiguous or objectively testable. Check completeness against the documented goals, success metrics, scope, requirement categories, assumptions, and constraints; record missing information as open questions for resolution. Check ambiguity by asking whether stakeholders can interpret the statement the same way; replace vague wording with plain, outcome-focused language and measurable thresholds where possible. Check testability by identifying an executable test and an objective pass/fail result for each stated condition; revise a condition if its satisfaction depends on subjective judgment.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Present the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions to stakeholders, capturing agreement or requested changes. That addresses validation of the intended business need. Separately verify the written requirement. Check completeness against the documented goals, success metrics, scope, categories, assumptions, and constraints. If the operating conditions are missing, record an open question rather than assuming them.

For ambiguity, ask whether stakeholders interpret “fast” the same way. In this hypothetical case, they clarify the requirement as “During normal dispatch preparation, the current instructions for a selected order are displayed within two seconds.” The condition and threshold are example decisions made by these stakeholders. For testability, identify an executable test: select an order in the stated conditions, measure the time until its current instructions appear, and compare that time with two seconds. The pass/fail result is objective; “it felt fast” is not.

The review therefore has two different outputs: agreement about the intended need, and wording that has been checked for completeness, ambiguity, and testability. Keep unresolved questions visible until the missing information is resolved.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Approval does not by itself prove that a sentence is unambiguous or testable. Nor does a precise threshold prove the requirement serves the intended business need. Validation and verification address different questions, so one cannot stand in for the other.

teaching_notes: Keep the validation/verification distinction explicit; do not invent mandatory test tooling.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose stakeholders struggle to explain what they need on a delivery-instruction screen. Instead of implementing the screen, draw a simple representation for discussion. A low-fidelity prototype can be inexpensive and relatively simple while still letting stakeholders explore a design.

teaching_blocks.title: Prototyping and Wireframing for Requirements Elicitation
teaching_blocks.content: A low-fidelity prototype is an inexpensive, relatively simple representation used to explore and test a design.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Sketch a wireframe by drawing the screen’s main content areas and controls without detailed visual styling. Use a prototype to gather feedback about a design before investing in a fully implemented version.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this example, sketch a page with an order identifier at the top, a large area for current instructions, and controls labeled “Select order” and “Confirm instructions.” These labels and areas are invented design choices for the exercise. Leave out detailed colors, typography, and visual styling. The wireframe’s job here is to represent the main content areas and controls, not to establish the final appearance.

Use the sketch to gather feedback before investing in a fully implemented version. A dispatcher might point to the instruction area and ask for the last amendment to be visible; another might explain that the confirmation control does not match their intended task. Record what the feedback reveals rather than treating every drawn control as an agreed requirement. The representation gives stakeholders something concrete to respond to while the design is still being explored. After discussion, the useful output is feedback about the design and needs it surfaces, not a claim that the screen is complete simply because all its boxes have labels.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A wireframe need not look like a finished interface. Adding detailed styling is not what makes this low-fidelity elicitation useful. Also distinguish the proposed design from the feedback collected about it: a sketched control is not automatically an agreed requirement.

video_need.reason: Drawing and revising a simple screen makes low-fidelity content areas, controls, and feedback tangible.

teaching_notes: Keep implementation and detailed UI design out of scope.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the team has agreed on the problem “Dispatch staff cannot find current delivery instructions.” The brainstorming goal is to generate alternative ideas for addressing that problem, not to decide immediately which idea wins.

teaching_blocks.title: Brainstorming
teaching_blocks.content: Brainstorming generates alternative ideas for a shared problem.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: State the session’s problem and goal, set a time limit, choose a facilitator, and record contributed ideas. Keep idea generation separate from judging ideas so participants can explore possibilities.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
State the problem and goal to the participants. For this hypothetical session, choose a facilitator, set a fifteen-minute limit, and prepare a place to record ideas. Contributors suggest a single instruction summary, a clearer amendment label, or a revised handoff between sales and dispatch. Record those contributed ideas so the discussion does not depend on remembering who said what.

Keep generation separate from judgment. If a participant responds to the first suggestion with “That will never work,” the facilitator can return the session to generating alternatives and leave evaluation for a separate discussion. This does not mean every idea must later be selected. It means the current activity is exploration, so an idea is recorded before it is judged.

At the end, the result is a set of alternatives connected to the same shared problem. The example ideas are possibilities, not recommended solutions. The distinction matters for a BA: a session aimed at generating ideas should not be described as if it had already established requirements or chosen an implementation. The facilitator, limit, and record provide a concrete frame for that exploration.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Separating generation from judgment is not the same as promising to implement every suggestion. Brainstorming produces alternatives for a shared problem. A session that immediately debates each contribution is mixing the two activities rather than preserving the stated separation.

teaching_notes: Avoid adding evaluation methods not taught by this concept.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an order-service team wants to hear how dispatch staff feel about a proposed instruction summary. A focus group is a moderated discussion of attitudes and opinions. Prepare a moderator script around specific issues: whether the summary feels clear, which information participants consider important, and where their preferences differ.

teaching_blocks.title: Focus Groups
teaching_blocks.content: A focus group is a moderated discussion that gathers participants’ attitudes and opinions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Prepare a moderator script with specific issues and goals for the information to be gathered. Keep discussion on topic, invite all participants to contribute, and prevent one participant from dominating. Record the opinions and disagreements expressed in the discussion without treating those stated preferences as evidence of actual product use.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
In the hypothetical discussion, one participant says the latest amendment should be most prominent; another prefers the complete instruction history. Record both opinions and the disagreement. Invite quieter participants to contribute and keep the conversation on the script’s issues. If one participant takes over, guide the discussion so their view does not become the only view captured.

The resulting record might say, “Participants disagreed about showing a summary versus a complete history,” with the preferences they expressed. It should not say, “Dispatchers use summaries during actual work,” because that behavior was not established by this discussion. The group’s stated preferences can inform requirements exploration without being relabeled as observation.

For the BA, the practical output is a supported account of attitudes, including disagreement. The moderator’s script keeps the information goal visible, while balanced participation lets more than one perspective be expressed. The invented design choices in this example are prompts for discussion, not a finding that either choice is the correct solution.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A focus group does not become evidence of actual product use merely because participants describe what they prefer. Keep stated opinions and disagreements as such. Moderating participation also does not require erasing disagreement to make the record look unanimous.

video_need.reason: A moderated discussion example can show inviting contributions and handling dominance while preserving differing opinions.

teaching_notes: Do not substitute group opinion for observation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine eliciting requirements for delivery-instruction access. A stakeholder reports that an external address feed may not be ready when needed. Record that known risk together with the blocker or dependency information supplied during elicitation, rather than leaving it outside the requirements discussion.

teaching_blocks.title: Risk Identification in Requirements
teaching_blocks.content: Gather information about known risks, blockers, and dependencies while eliciting requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A risk matrix evaluates a risk using its likelihood and impact. Assess likelihood and impact for each identified risk and use its matrix position to determine a risk level.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Assess its likelihood and impact. For this hypothetical matrix, the team labels likelihood low, medium, or high and impact low, medium, or high. Suppose the address-feed risk is assessed as medium likelihood and high impact. Place it at that intersection and use the matrix’s agreed risk-level labels to determine its level. The category boundaries are choices for this example; the concept does not supply a universal numerical formula or universal label for that cell.

A second risk might have high likelihood but low impact. Locate it separately rather than assuming frequency and consequence are the same thing. The matrix evaluates both dimensions, so your record should preserve the two assessments as well as the resulting level.

The useful requirements output is a list of identified risks, blockers, and dependencies with reasoned likelihood and impact assessments. It is not a promise that a risk will occur. Nor is merely drawing a grid enough: the assessment and the matrix position must be connected to each identified risk.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Likelihood is not impact. A frequently occurring inconvenience and a less likely severe disruption can occupy different matrix positions. Do not invent a universal score from category words; use the risk-level interpretation of the matrix being used.

video_need.reason: Placing risks on two independent axes makes likelihood, impact, and the resulting matrix position clear.

teaching_notes: Keep mitigation frameworks and unsupported scoring formulas out of this explanation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the business wants fewer dispatch delays caused by unclear instructions. That broader outcome is a business requirement; it is not yet a detailed description of every action a system must perform.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Requirements Documents
teaching_blocks.content: Business requirements express the broader business goal or outcome the work should support.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A requirements document can contain a project summary, goals and success metrics, in-scope and out-of-scope items, requirements, assumptions, and constraints. Organize the elicited requirements in that shared structure and review them with approvers to agree what will be delivered.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Organize a shared requirements document around the effort. In this hypothetical document, the summary describes the instruction-access problem, the goal is fewer clarification delays, and a success metric is a stated target for dispatch preparation time. The scope includes the North branch and excludes vehicle purchasing. Record the elicited requirements, along with assumptions such as availability of the current instruction record and constraints such as a required approval. These example entries illustrate the shared structure; they do not prescribe the same content for every initiative.

Review the organized requirements with approvers to agree what will be delivered. If an approver questions the branch boundary or success target, capture the issue rather than treating the document’s existence as agreement. The document gathers the business outcome and supporting delivery context in one place so the review has something specific to consider.

A reader should be able to distinguish the reason for the work from the items expected within its scope. For example, “reduce clarification delays” states the outcome, while the requirement entries describe the agreed needs supporting it. Keep that distinction visible instead of replacing the business goal with a long feature list.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A business requirements document is not made complete by a title or a feature list. The broad outcome and the supporting context need to be clear, and the elicited requirements still need review with approvers. The listed sections are possible contents, not a closed mandatory template.

teaching_notes: Preserve “can contain”; keep functional specification detail for its own concept.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the business outcome is fewer dispatch delays. A functional requirement supporting that outcome might be “Display the current delivery instructions when a dispatcher selects an order.” This describes what the deliverable must do, rather than restating the outcome or saying how quickly it should operate.

teaching_blocks.title: Functional Specifications
teaching_blocks.content: Functional requirements state what the deliverable must do.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Document the expected functions separately from the broader business outcome and from how the solution should perform. Write a detailed functional specification entry with the initiating event and input values, the expected system response, resulting outputs, and applicable preconditions, postconditions, or exception behavior.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Expand it into a hypothetical specification entry. The initiating event is selecting an order; the input is the selected order identifier. The expected response is to retrieve and display that order’s current instructions, and the output is the displayed instruction text. A precondition could be that the order exists; a postcondition could be that its current instructions are visible. For an unknown identifier, the example exception behavior is to display a clear not-found result instead of instruction text. These are example requirements, not claims about an existing product.

The detailed entry now gives a reader the behavior for both the ordinary situation and the relevant exception. Keep the broader business outcome in its own place and document performance expectations separately. “Reduce delays” explains why the work matters, but it does not tell the reader what happens when an identifier is selected.

The practical skill is moving from a vague function label such as “instruction access” to an explicit event, inputs, response, outputs, and applicable conditions. Do not invent preconditions or exceptions silently; in real elicitation those details need to be established for the requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A functional specification is not a list of business aspirations. Nor does “fast lookup” fully describe the function. Specify the expected behavior and applicable conditions separately from the broader outcome and the way the solution should perform.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce implementation APIs, database commands, or technical design.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a dispatcher needs current instructions before releasing an order. An example story is “As a dispatcher, I want to see the current delivery instructions for a selected order, so that I can prepare the correct dispatch.” The persona, need, and purpose are visible without turning the story into a technical design.

teaching_blocks.title: User Stories with Acceptance Criteria
teaching_blocks.content: A user story describes a desired outcome from a user’s perspective.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a story as “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].” to state the user, need, and purpose. Acceptance criteria describe specific conditions that must be satisfied for the story to be accepted. Write each acceptance scenario on separate lines using “Given …”, “When …”, and “Then …” in that order. Given sets the initial context or precondition, When describes the action or event, and Then states an expected result observable to the user or an external system.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
The story still needs specific conditions for acceptance. One hypothetical scenario is:
Given an existing order has current delivery instructions
When the dispatcher selects that order
Then the current instructions are displayed for the dispatcher.

Given establishes the initial context, When names the action, and Then states an observable result. Keep the lines in that order. A second scenario could address an unknown order:
Given an order identifier does not exist
When the dispatcher selects that identifier
Then a not-found result is displayed.

These conditions describe what must be satisfied for this story to be accepted in the example. They do not claim the two scenarios cover every need in a real system. Discuss the relevant conditions rather than assuming the story sentence supplies them all.

The BA’s work is to connect the user-perspective outcome with specific acceptance conditions. A reader should be able to see who benefits and then identify the result to check. “The feature works correctly” would not provide the same observable expectation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The user-story sentence and acceptance criteria are related but not interchangeable. The sentence communicates the desired user outcome; the scenarios state specific conditions for acceptance. A Then line should describe an observable result, not merely say that the action was performed.

teaching_notes: Keep stories user-centered; do not introduce later refinement checklists yet.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a dispatcher asking an order service for current instructions. In a use case, “dispatcher” is the actor role interacting with the subject; it is not the name of one particular employee. Another system could also act as an actor if it interacts with the subject.

teaching_blocks.title: Use Case Specifications
teaching_blocks.content: A use case specifies behavior that provides an observable result of value to an actor or other stakeholder.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: An actor represents a role interacting with the subject and may be a person or another system. Describe a use case’s behavior in natural language with relevant preconditions and postconditions. Include the basic interaction and relevant variations, exceptional behavior, or error handling.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical use case, state the valued result as obtaining current delivery instructions. Describe the basic interaction in natural language: the dispatcher identifies an order, the service finds its current instructions, and the service presents them. A relevant precondition is that the dispatcher has an order to identify. A postcondition for the successful interaction is that the current instructions have been presented.

Include relevant variations and exceptions. For example, if the identifier is unknown, describe the not-found response. If no instructions are recorded, describe the agreed response for that situation rather than leaving the basic interaction to imply success. The conditions and responses are invented here to show the specification’s structure, not existing tool behavior.

The useful output is an account of behavior that gives an actor or stakeholder an observable result of value, together with the relevant conditions and alternate behavior. A short label such as “view instructions” names an interaction but leaves its behavior unspecified. Conversely, the specification can remain in natural language; this concept does not require programming the interaction.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An actor is a role, not necessarily a human or a named employee. A use case also needs more than its successful path when variations or error behavior are relevant. Include those behaviors and conditions rather than letting a success-only description stand for every situation.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Avoid unsupported use-case templates or UML symbols.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose requirement R-12 says a dispatcher must see current instructions for a selected order. Its originating business need is reducing clarification delays. A traceability matrix keeps that connection alongside links to the work that fulfills and checks the requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Requirements Traceability
teaching_blocks.content: Requirements traceability maintains links from initial business needs through design, development, and testing to the work that fulfills the requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Construct an RTM with a row for each requirement identifier and columns for its originating business need or source, related design artifact, and test-case identifiers; populate these with references to the actual artifacts rather than unlinked descriptions. When a requirement changes, follow its links to identify affected work items that need updating. Review the RTM for missing required links: a requirement without a source link is orphaned from its business justification, and a missing design or test link is a coverage gap when that artifact is required for the stage being reviewed.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Create a row for R-12 with columns for the originating need or source, related design artifact, and test-case identifiers. In this hypothetical record, link the source to Need-3, the design to Design-7, and the tests to Test-21 and Test-22. These labels stand for actual referenced artifacts in the exercise. A cell saying “some testing” is not the same as a reference to the test artifacts.

Now suppose R-12 changes to include an amended-instruction indicator. Follow its links to identify related design, development, and testing work that may need updating. The matrix helps you find affected work; the requirement change should not remain isolated in its own paragraph.

Review link coverage for the stage being considered. No source link leaves the requirement orphaned from its business justification. A missing design or test link is a coverage gap when that artifact is required at that stage. This qualification matters: do not demand a later-stage artifact merely because its column exists. The practical result is connected requirements and stage-appropriate evidence, not just a table filled with descriptions.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A matrix is not traceability merely because it has columns. Its entries must reference the supporting artifacts. Also distinguish a missing required link from a link to an artifact not yet required at the reviewed stage; the latter qualification should not be discarded.

video_need.reason: Following links from a changed requirement to source, design, and tests makes change impact and missing coverage visible.

teaching_notes: Do not imply every artifact must exist at every stage.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine R-12 has been agreed for delivery, then a stakeholder proposes adding an amended-instruction indicator. Requirements life cycle management keeps that revision and its decision visible instead of silently replacing the current requirement.

teaching_blocks.title: Requirements Life Cycle Management
teaching_blocks.content: Requirements documentation needs updating as development and learning change the understanding of the work.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Track the current program status and keep requirements linked to current work-item status. For a changed requirement, identify and update related work through its traceability links. Use a customized requirement workflow to distinguish draft (under preparation or review), approved (agreed for delivery), change under review (a proposed revision awaiting a decision), and retired (no longer current); make approval, revision review, and retirement explicit status transitions rather than silently overwriting the current requirement. For a proposed change, record the affected requirement and change request, review its risks and expected outcomes, record the approval decision and status, then document the implemented change and its results. When the requirement is documented on a Confluence page, modifying that page creates a new version; record the current workflow status in the document, and use More options > Page History to inspect version numbers and compare the revision with the preceding version.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Use an explicit customized workflow. In this example, draft means preparation or review, approved means agreed for delivery, change under review means a proposed revision awaiting a decision, and retired means no longer current. Record R-12’s current status and link it to current work-item status. A proposed revision is not the same as an approved replacement.

Record the affected requirement and change request, review the risks and expected outcomes, and record the approval decision and status. If approved and implemented, document the change and its results. Follow traceability links to identify and update related work. If the requirement is retired, make that transition explicit too rather than leaving an obsolete requirement looking current.

When the requirement lives on a Confluence page, modifying the page creates a new version. Record workflow status in the document, then use More options > Page History to inspect version numbers and compare the revision with the preceding version. Page versions show revisions; the documented workflow status shows whether a revision is draft, agreed, under review, or retired. Keep those two ideas separate.

The BA’s record should let a reader understand the current requirement, the proposed change, the decision, and the resulting work without guessing from whichever paragraph was edited last.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A newer page version does not by itself mean an approved requirement. Approval, revision review, and retirement are explicit workflow transitions. Likewise, editing requirement text without following its traceability links leaves the related work unaddressed.

video_need.reason: A status-and-version walkthrough can distinguish requirement decisions from page revisions and show comparison through Page History.

teaching_notes: Treat workflow as customized, not a built-in universal Confluence status machine.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a requirement says the service must display delivery instructions. That describes a function. A request that the display be “fast” describes a performance expectation, but its wording does not yet supply a measurable target.

teaching_blocks.title: Non-Functional Requirements
teaching_blocks.content: Nonfunctional requirements describe how the solution should perform or operate rather than the functions it must provide.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Make the performance expectation measurable by stating a concrete numerical target rather than a vague request for good performance.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical situation, stakeholders specify “Current delivery instructions are displayed within two seconds when a dispatcher selects an existing order during normal dispatch preparation.” The numerical target replaces the vague performance word. The function remains displaying instructions; the performance condition says how the solution should perform when doing so.

Compare the two statements side by side. “Display the instructions” answers what the deliverable must do. “Within two seconds under the stated conditions” answers a question about performance or operation. The two-second threshold is example stakeholder input, not a universal definition of acceptable lookup performance.

When documenting the requirement, preserve the concrete target instead of summarizing it back to “good performance.” The measurable expectation gives the requirements discussion something specific to agree about. In this example, a measured three-second display does not satisfy the stated two-second expectation even if a participant describes it as reasonably quick. That is the practical difference between a numerical target and a favorable adjective.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Here, nonfunctional distinguishes how the solution performs or operates from the functions it provides. “User-friendly and fast” is not a concrete numerical performance target. Do not confuse a positive description with a measurable expectation.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Focus on the supported performance distinction; avoid unsupported taxonomies.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine mapping the people involved in changing delivery-instruction access. Dispatch staff use the deliverable; sales staff provide instruction input; an operations manager approves the change; a sponsor funds it. Customer-support staff may be affected by changes in clarification work. These are hypothetical roles, not a fixed stakeholder list for every initiative.

teaching_blocks.title: Stakeholder Identification and Classification
teaching_blocks.content: A stakeholder is someone interested in the work or someone whose involvement is needed to complete it.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify people who use, provide input to, approve, fund, or are affected by the deliverable. Classify stakeholders as directly involved or affected, indirectly affected or consulted, and reviewers or approvers, noting that roles can overlap. Record each stakeholder’s role and assess their interest and power over the work.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Record who uses, provides input to, approves, funds, or is affected by the deliverable. Classify their involvement: some are directly involved or affected, some indirectly affected or consulted, and some reviewers or approvers. Roles can overlap. For example, the operations manager might be directly affected by dispatch outcomes and also an approver. Do not force that person into just one category if both roles apply.

Record each stakeholder’s role and assess their interest and power over the work. In this example, a dispatcher may have strong interest in usable instructions but less decision power than the approving manager. The manager’s formal approval role does not tell you everything about their degree of interest, so keep the two assessments visible.

The output is more useful than a contact list: it explains why each person or group belongs in the analysis and how they relate to the deliverable. Begin with involvement and effect rather than assuming only senior people count as stakeholders. People whose work changes can belong even when they do not approve the budget.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A stakeholder is not only a sponsor or decision-maker. Interest, needed involvement, and being affected can all matter. Classification categories can overlap, so assigning one role should not erase another role the same person actually holds.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not teach the matrix’s engagement quadrants before its own entry.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the operations manager has high power over an instruction-access change and high interest in its outcome. Dispatch staff have high interest but lower power. A finance approver has high power but limited day-to-day interest, while an indirectly affected group has low power and low interest. These are example assessments, not assumptions about everyone with those titles.

teaching_blocks.title: Influence-Interest Matrix
teaching_blocks.content: Plot stakeholders on a grid with separate low-to-high power and interest axes.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Manage high-power, high-interest stakeholders closely. Keep high-power, low-interest stakeholders satisfied. Keep low-power, high-interest stakeholders informed. Monitor low-power, low-interest stakeholders with less intensive engagement.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Plot them on a grid with a low-to-high power axis and a separate low-to-high interest axis. The manager’s high/high position calls for close management. The high-power, low-interest approver should be kept satisfied. Dispatch staff in the low-power, high-interest position should be kept informed. The low/low group is monitored with less intensive engagement.

Read each position using both axes. Low power does not imply low interest, and high power does not automatically imply high interest. In the example, dispatch staff and the finance approver occupy different quadrants even though both matter to the initiative.

The matrix turns the assessed combination into an engagement approach. It does not identify stakeholders on its own or prescribe a universal message frequency. If you describe the dispatch group as needing information, point back to its assessed low-power/high-interest position rather than simply claiming all users belong there. The practical skill is matching the action to the plotted combination while keeping the assessments explicit.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Do not collapse power and interest into one importance label. “Keep informed” and “keep satisfied” belong to different combinations. A job title alone is not a substitute for assessing and plotting the stakeholder’s power and interest in this work.

video_need.reason: Plotting examples across two axes makes the four engagement approaches and their contrasts clear.

teaching_notes: Keep message schedules for engagement planning; teach the axes and four approaches.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the task is reviewing delivery-instruction requirements. A hypothetical RACI row assigns the BA as Responsible for doing the review preparation, the operations manager as Accountable for the task’s completion, dispatch and sales as Consulted, and the sponsor as Informed.

teaching_blocks.title: RACI Matrix
teaching_blocks.content: A RACI chart assigns roles by task to clarify who does work and who owns the outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Responsible identifies the person or people doing the work. Accountable identifies the one person ultimately answerable for a task’s completion. Consulted identifies people whose input is needed, using two-way communication. Informed identifies people kept updated, using one-way communication. List tasks against stakeholders and assign the appropriate R, A, C, or I entries, checking that each task has one accountable owner.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Read each letter as a different relationship to this task. Responsible identifies the person or people doing the work. Accountable identifies the one person ultimately answerable for completion. Consulted participants provide input through two-way communication; Informed participants receive updates through one-way communication. The row therefore does not simply mark who attends a meeting.

Build the chart by listing tasks against stakeholders and assigning appropriate R, A, C, or I entries. For a second example task, “Prepare an instruction-access demonstration,” the role assignments might differ. Do not carry the first row’s assignments over merely because the same people are involved. Check that each task has one accountable owner.

In the first row, asking dispatch for input fits C; sending the sponsor a progress update fits I. If two people are marked A for the same task, the row does not meet the one-accountable-owner check. Resolve the ownership assignment rather than leaving two competing A entries. The useful result is task-specific clarity about work, ownership, consultation, and updates, not a general ranking of stakeholder seniority.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Responsible and Accountable are not interchangeable. Several people can do the work, while the task has one ultimately answerable owner. Consulted also differs from Informed: input requires two-way communication; receiving an update is one-way.

video_need.reason: Building and checking task rows makes R/A ownership and C/I communication differences visible.

teaching_notes: Keep assignments hypothetical; do not prescribe the BA as accountable for business approval.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose stakeholder analysis shows an operations manager with high power and interest and dispatch staff with high interest but lower power. Engagement planning turns those assessments into specific ongoing communication actions rather than leaving them as labels on a grid.

teaching_blocks.title: Stakeholder Engagement Planning
teaching_blocks.content: A communication plan turns stakeholder analysis into specific ongoing engagement actions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: For each stakeholder group, specify the communication goal, channel, frequency, and owner. Match communication intensity to stakeholder power and interest and review whether the approach is effective.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical plan, the manager’s communication goal is to resolve scope decisions. The channel is a short decision meeting, the frequency is weekly during requirements review, and the owner is the BA preparing the materials. Dispatch staff’s goal is to understand current requirements and supply feedback; the channel is a shared update and discussion, with a stated frequency and owner. These channels and timings are examples chosen for this situation, not a mandatory schedule.

For every stakeholder group, make the goal, channel, frequency, and owner explicit. Then check whether the planned intensity fits the group’s power and interest. An assessment has practical value only when it informs actual engagement choices.

Review effectiveness too. If a group remains unclear about what is being agreed, consider whether the approach is meeting its communication goal. The plan is not merely proof that messages were sent. It should connect who is involved, why communication is needed, how it will occur, and who owns it. The example stays within communication planning; it does not transfer business decision authority to the person sending the update.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A list of channels is not yet an engagement plan. Each group needs a communication goal, frequency, and owner as well. Sending an update also does not by itself establish that the approach is effective; review it against the intended engagement goal.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Use example frequencies only, not universal stakeholder rules.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a requirements meeting where one sales representative answers every question before dispatch staff can speak. The facilitator’s task is to support the group’s collaborative process, not to let the loudest contribution become the whole record.

teaching_blocks.title: Meeting and Workshop Facilitation
teaching_blocks.content: A workshop facilitator supports the group’s process by planning, guiding, and managing collaborative work.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use an agenda whose activities and allotted time support the meeting’s goals. Redirect dominating contributions toward shared goals or invite other participants to balance the discussion. Use silent individual contributions when verbal discussion prevents equitable participation.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Plan an agenda with activities and allotted time that support the meeting’s goal. For this example, the goal is to clarify delivery-instruction needs, so allocate time for individual input, shared discussion, and consolidating the needs. During discussion, redirect a dominating contribution toward the shared goal or invite others to contribute: “We have the sales perspective; what does dispatch need at that point?” This keeps guidance connected to the work rather than making it a contest between participants.

If verbal discussion still prevents equitable participation, use silent individual contributions. Participants could each write the instruction information they need before the group discusses it. That is an example of the supported technique, not a claim that silent writing is required in every meeting.

The facilitator plans, guides, and manages the process so the group can work collaboratively. The useful result is not merely finishing every agenda item on time: activities and time need to support the goals, and discussion needs room for balanced contributions. Keep the facilitation intervention focused on participation and shared purpose rather than deciding whose requirement is correct on the group’s behalf.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Facilitation is not the same as speaking most or choosing the group’s solution. Redirecting dominance and inviting input support the collaborative process. Silent contributions are an option when verbal discussion prevents equitable participation, not a compulsory ritual for every workshop.

video_need.reason: A facilitated discussion demonstration can show redirection, invitations, and a switch to silent contributions.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce consensus or voting as substitutes for balanced participation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose sales wants very few fields on a delivery-instruction form, while dispatch wants enough information to avoid clarification calls. Their goals and measures of success differ: one emphasizes easy entry, the other complete dispatch information. Naming that difference is more useful than presenting one side’s preferred design as an isolated solution.

teaching_blocks.title: Consensus Building and Conflict Resolution
teaching_blocks.content: Different stakeholders may have conflicting goals and different measures of success.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Build shared understanding by involving stakeholders in discussion of goals and evidence rather than presenting an isolated solution. Forced ranking or dot voting can help a group move toward consensus.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Bring stakeholders into discussion of the goals and evidence. For this hypothetical case, examine examples of instruction entry and clarification work together. Ask what each group is trying to achieve and which evidence relates to that goal. The purpose is shared understanding of the competing needs, not hiding the disagreement behind a vague claim that everyone wants a better process.

Forced ranking or dot voting can help the group move toward consensus. For example, participants could rank the information needs being discussed or place dots beside the needs they consider most important. The technique supports movement toward agreement; a ranking does not itself establish that the selected solution is correct.

The useful BA contribution is a discussion in which stakeholders can see one another’s goals and evidence before moving toward a shared position. Keep any remaining disagreement visible rather than announcing consensus merely because a voting activity took place. The example fields and goals are hypothetical prompts for that discussion.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Consensus building is not presenting a ready-made solution and asking for compliance. Voting or ranking can help, but the supported claim is that these techniques can move a group toward consensus—not that a vote guarantees complete agreement or correctness.

video_need.reason: A group discussion example can show how goals and evidence are surfaced before a ranking or voting activity.

teaching_notes: Avoid unsupported negotiation frameworks or claims that majority vote is binding.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine representing a simple dispatch process: an order arrives, staff prepare it, a decision determines whether clarification is needed, and the path ends after dispatch preparation. BPMN notation gives each kind of element a distinct visual role rather than drawing every step as the same box.

teaching_blocks.title: BPMN 2.0 Core Notation Elements
teaching_blocks.content: An event is something that happens during a process and is drawn as a circle.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A task is an atomic activity and is drawn as a rounded rectangle. A gateway controls branching and convergence of sequence flows and is drawn as a diamond. Sequence flow is a solid line with a solid arrowhead indicating the order of activities within a process. Message flow is a dashed line with an open arrowhead and open circle showing messages between separate participants. Draw activities and appropriate events or gateways, connecting execution order with sequence flows and communication between participants with message flows. Select a thin single-circle start event to show where a process starts, a thin double-circle intermediate event for something occurring between its start and end, and a thick single-circle end event to show where a process path ends.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Draw the arrival as a thin single-circle start event and “Prepare order” as a rounded-rectangle task. Draw the branching decision as a diamond gateway. Connect execution order within the process using solid lines with solid arrowheads: these are sequence flows. If something occurs between start and end, select a thin double-circle intermediate event; mark the end of a process path with a thick single-circle end event. The example does not require every event type on every path.

Suppose dispatch sends a request to a separate participant, such as an external delivery service. Represent that communication with a dashed message flow having an open circle and open arrowhead, not with the solid sequence flow used for execution order. The diagram now distinguishes something happening, an atomic activity, routing, and communication between participants.

When reading it back, name both the element and what it represents in this process. “Diamond” describes the shape; “gateway controlling branching and convergence” explains its function. Keep the notation tied to the work rather than memorizing disconnected shapes.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A sequence flow and a message flow do different jobs. Solid sequence arrows indicate execution order within a process; dashed message flows show communication between separate participants. Start, intermediate, and end events are also distinguished by their circle outlines, not all drawn identically.

video_need.reason: Drawing the process reveals shape distinctions, event outlines, execution order, and separate-participant communication.

teaching_notes: Teach only supported core shapes and flows; avoid gateway subtypes, pools, lanes, and advanced markers.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose dispatch work currently begins when an order arrives and ends when preparation is complete. You want a record of that existing behavior, not a cleaner version of what you hope staff will do.

teaching_blocks.title: As-Is Process Modeling
teaching_blocks.content: An as-is process map records the current process rather than a proposed redesign.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the process’s start and end, collect information about its steps and decisions, and determine their sequence. Represent the observed activities and routing with BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows. Review the map with those who perform the process to refine its accuracy.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify the start and end, then collect information about the actual steps and decisions. In this hypothetical process, staff read the order, check instructions, decide whether clarification is needed, request clarification if necessary, and prepare dispatch. Determine the sequence and routing from that information. Represent the activities with BPMN tasks, use appropriate events and gateways, and connect execution order with sequence flows.

If clarification is inconvenient, keep it in the as-is map when it is part of the current process. Removing it because it looks inefficient would change the map from a current-state record to a proposal. Review the map with people who perform the process. They may explain that clarification happens before another step, or that the map omitted an activity. Refine the map to reflect their review.

The practical output is a current-process model with a supported sequence and routing. Accuracy is the immediate aim here. A later improvement discussion can use that baseline, but the as-is map should not silently merge observed behavior with desired changes.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: As-is means current, not ideal. A troublesome step still belongs if it is part of current work. Review with the people performing the process refines accuracy; it is not permission to replace current behavior with a proposed redesign.

video_need.reason: Building and reviewing a current-state BPMN map makes observed sequencing and routing concrete.

teaching_notes: Keep improvements as a later comparison, not embedded in the as-is map.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the current dispatch map includes a separate instruction-sheet lookup and a clarification request. The team proposes a future process in which current instructions are available at the order step. A to-be map shows that intended future behavior, not a claim that the change has already happened.

teaching_blocks.title: To-Be Process Modeling
teaching_blocks.content: A future-state process map shows how the process is intended to work after improvement.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use the current-state map to identify improvements and draw a revised map reflecting the proposed changes. Use BPMN tasks, events, gateways, and sequence flows to represent the revised activities and routing.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Use the current-state map to identify the proposed improvements. In this hypothetical redesign, replace the separate lookup with “Read current instructions on order,” and revise the routing for clarification according to the proposed behavior. Draw the changed activities using BPMN tasks, appropriate events and gateways, and sequence flows. Keep the revised map understandable as a complete proposed process rather than a few isolated change labels.

Read the old and revised sequences separately. The as-is sequence records the current lookup; the to-be sequence reflects the proposed instruction-access change. Their different meanings matter even when both use the same BPMN shapes.

The useful output is a future-state map that explicitly represents intended activities and routing after improvement. The example is a proposal, not evidence of achieved efficiency. A revised diagram can communicate how the process is meant to work while leaving implementation and actual results to their own work.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: To-be does not mean already operating. Do not describe a proposed route as observed behavior or assume that redrawing a process proves an improvement has been achieved. The model represents the intended future state.

video_need.reason: A before-and-proposed-after drawing shows how activities and routing change between maps.

teaching_notes: Use the current map as input; avoid claiming measured benefits from a proposal.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the dispatch map shows orders accumulating before an approval step. A delay label alone does not establish the full bottleneck explanation. In this hypothetical case, the step can handle ten orders per hour while fifteen arrive, and the waiting work grows. Annotate the map with that capacity and accumulating-work evidence: the step cannot keep pace and limits the workflow’s throughput.

teaching_blocks.title: Process Gap and Bottleneck Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: Process mapping can expose bottlenecks, redundant efforts, and unnecessary steps.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect the mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles that impede efficient flow. Compare current-state and future-state maps to identify specific differences and potential efficiency gains. List the specific steps or handoffs where the map shows delay, redundancy, or missing work, and review these findings with process stakeholders. Identify a bottleneck as a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing work to accumulate and limiting the whole workflow’s throughput, and cite the observed capacity, throughput, or accumulating-work evidence in the diagram annotation.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect other mapped steps and handoffs for obstacles, redundancy, or missing work. Perhaps the same instructions are copied at two handoffs. List the specific steps where the map shows those issues and review the findings with process stakeholders. Do not group every issue under “bottleneck” merely because it is inconvenient.

Compare current-state and future-state maps too. If the proposal removes one copying step, identify that concrete difference and discuss its potential efficiency gain. A map comparison identifies a proposed difference; it is not itself a measured result.

The output should connect each finding to a location in the process and supporting evidence. For the approval bottleneck, the key evidence is capacity that cannot keep pace, accumulated work, and the resulting throughput limitation. For redundant copying, the finding is repeated effort. These distinctions make the analysis more informative than marking every slow-looking box red.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Not every delay is a bottleneck. The supported bottleneck definition requires a capacity-limited step that cannot keep pace, causing accumulation and limiting throughput. Also label future-state efficiency gains as potential until supported by actual results.

video_need.reason: Showing work accumulating at a capacity-limited step and comparing mapped handoffs clarifies bottleneck evidence.

teaching_notes: Keep capacity examples hypothetical; distinguish bottlenecks from redundancy and missing work.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the process map shows dispatch instructions copied twice before preparation. The team investigates that repeated effort as a possible non-value-adding step. Lean improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve the value delivered by the process; the example is about examining a specific source of waste, not removing work simply because it takes time.

teaching_blocks.title: Process Improvement Techniques
teaching_blocks.content: Lean process improvement aims to eliminate waste and improve value delivered by a process.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Inspect a process for non-value-adding steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste. Agree an improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects to continue improving the process.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the copying steps and propose a change that removes or reduces the identified waste. In this hypothetical situation, the team proposes using the current instruction record instead of making a second copy. Agree the improvement action with the team, implement it, and review its effects.
