The review might examine whether the repeated copying was reduced and whether the process now delivers the intended value more effectively. Those are questions for the review, not results you can infer from the proposal alone. If the effects show further issues, continue improving the process rather than treating the first change as the final answer.

The BA’s analysis connects an observed process feature, identified waste, an agreed action, and a review of effects. The technique remains grounded in the work: “remove a box from the map” is less informative than explaining which non-value-adding activity is being reduced and then checking the change.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Improvement is not synonymous with deleting as many steps as possible. Inspect for identified non-value-adding work, agree an action, and review its effects after implementation. A proposed simplification is not yet evidence that value or efficiency improved.

video_need.reason: A process example can show identified repeated effort, the proposed change, and what would be reviewed afterward.

teaching_notes: Do not add unsupported Lean waste categories or mandatory improvement cycles.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose stakeholders say amended delivery instructions require supervisor approval. That approval governs what the deliverable must allow; it should not remain an informal comment outside the requirements record.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Rules Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: Requirements documentation includes assumptions and constraints that govern the work.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Capture required approvals and operating constraints explicitly when documenting what the deliverable must do.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
In this hypothetical entry, document “An amended instruction requires supervisor approval before dispatch preparation continues.” Record the operating constraint explicitly alongside the required behavior. If the team assumes that a supervisor is available during dispatch hours, capture that assumption too rather than leaving it hidden in the sentence.

The distinction is practical: a requested function might be displaying or amending instructions, while the governing approval or constraint limits how the work may proceed. Make those assumptions, constraints, and approvals visible in the requirement record.

Read the requirement record back to stakeholders with the approval made visible. A description that says only “Users can amend instructions” omits the stated governing condition in this example. The useful output is explicit required approval and operating-constraint information linked to what the deliverable must do. The supervisor rule is invented for the exercise, not a general policy for order services.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An approval rule should not be left as background prose while the function is documented without it. Capture governing assumptions and constraints explicitly. Do not invent company policies or a complete business-rule classification beyond what the requirements evidence supports.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Coverage is narrow: focus on explicit approvals, assumptions, and constraints; do not expand to an unsupported rule taxonomy.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a hypothetical policy with two conditions: whether an order is urgent and whether approval is present. The written rule says an urgent approved order may proceed; an urgent unapproved order requests approval; a nonurgent order may proceed regardless of approval.

teaching_blocks.title: Decision Tables
teaching_blocks.content: A decision table records how combinations of conditions produce outcomes, including complex logic such as business rules.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: To construct a decision table, put the conditions and resulting actions in rows and give each decision rule a column containing a unique condition combination and its associated actions. For a limited-entry decision table, mark a condition T when satisfied, F when not satisfied, and – when irrelevant to the outcome; mark an action X when it should occur and leave it blank when it should not occur. Check completeness by listing all condition combinations and confirming each feasible combination has a rule column with its resulting action; a feasible combination without a rule is a gap, while infeasible combinations can be removed. Check consistency by comparing the outcomes assigned to the same feasible condition combination across the written rules and table; incompatible outcomes for that combination expose a contradiction that needs resolution.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Construct a limited-entry decision table with condition rows “Urgent?” and “Approved?” and action rows “Proceed” and “Request approval.” Give each rule a column. Rule 1 has T/T and X for Proceed. Rule 2 has T/F and X for Request approval. Rule 3 has F/– and X for Proceed. Leave the other action cells blank. Here – means the approval condition is irrelevant to the nonurgent outcome, so Rule 3 covers F/T and F/F.

Check completeness by listing the feasible combinations T/T, T/F, F/T, and F/F. All four have an outcome in this example. If Rule 2 were missing, T/F would be a gap. Infeasible combinations could be removed in a different policy, but none are declared infeasible here.

Check consistency against the written rules. If another rule assigns Request approval instead of Proceed to T/T, the same feasible combination has incompatible outcomes. Record that contradiction for resolution rather than choosing one arbitrarily. The table’s job is to expose condition-to-action logic, including gaps and contradictions, not conceal uncertainty behind a neat grid.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A dash is not false: it means the condition is irrelevant to the outcome. Completeness and consistency are separate checks. A table can cover every feasible combination and still contradict the written rules by assigning incompatible outcomes to the same combination.

video_need.reason: Filling rule columns and checking every feasible combination makes dash expansion, gaps, and contradictions visible.

teaching_notes: Use conditions as rows and rules as columns; avoid reversing the brief convention.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a hypothetical dispatch decision first asks whether an order is urgent. If yes, it next asks whether approval is present. If no, it proceeds through the nonurgent outcome. A decision tree makes that sequence of choices and possible outcomes visible with branches.

teaching_blocks.title: Decision Trees
teaching_blocks.content: A decision tree represents choices and possible outcomes with branches.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Start with the initial decision, add branches for the possible answers, and continue with subsequent decisions and their outcomes.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Start with the initial decision “Urgent?” Add one branch for yes and another for no. On the yes branch, add the subsequent decision “Approval present?” and branches for its possible answers. The approved path ends at “Proceed”; the unapproved path ends at “Request approval.” In this exercise, the no-urgency branch ends at “Proceed.” These are invented policy outcomes, not general rules for dispatch.

Read a path from the initial decision through the relevant answers to its outcome. An urgent order without approval follows yes at the first decision and no at the second, reaching Request approval. This explanation ties branch labels to decisions instead of using unlabeled lines.

The useful output is sequential branching logic. Do not add a subsequent decision to every branch merely to make the drawing symmetrical; continue where the decision being represented requires it. The tree communicates choices and outcomes, not the statistical prediction methods that may use a similarly named structure elsewhere.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A branch represents a possible answer or choice leading onward; it is not just decoration around a list of outcomes. Keep the initial and subsequent decisions visible so the reader can follow the sequence. This is business decision logic, not a machine-learning lesson.

video_need.reason: Drawing and tracing one path makes ordered decisions, answer branches, and final outcomes easy to follow.

teaching_notes: Avoid decision-table completeness rules being silently recast as tree-specific facts.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a stakeholder saying, “We need to describe customers and their orders, including the customer name and each order’s requested delivery date.” Start by identifying the business things being described: Customer and Order. Then separate their descriptive properties.

teaching_blocks.title: Entities and Attributes
teaching_blocks.content: An entity is a business thing being described; its attributes are descriptive properties of that thing.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the business things that need describing and list the descriptive attributes needed for each.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical domain, list Customer attributes such as customer name and contact number, and Order attributes such as requested delivery date and instruction text. The attribute belongs to the thing it describes. A requested delivery date describes an order in this example, while customer name describes a customer.

Read another sentence: “Dispatch staff need the instruction text for an order.” It adds a descriptive need for Order rather than automatically introducing a new entity called InstructionText. The question is which business thing needs describing and which properties are needed for that description.

The output can remain a plain list of entities with attributes. This step does not require keys, relationship symbols, or a database implementation. Those details come later. Focus first on distinguishing a business thing from a descriptive property of that thing, using the narrative as evidence rather than adding every imaginable attribute. The resulting list should answer what the business needs to describe in this example.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An attribute is not automatically a separate entity because its name appears in a sentence. Ask whether it describes a business thing already identified. Conversely, do not merge unrelated business things into one vague entity just because they appear in the same narrative.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Keep keys and relationships for subsequent concepts; use ordinary business descriptions first.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a Customer table has rows for customers 101, 102, and 103. CustomerID is a candidate for the primary key if each row’s value is unique and not null. CustomerName is less suitable in an example where two different customers share the name “North Stores”: the repeated name would not uniquely identify each row.

teaching_blocks.title: Primary Keys
teaching_blocks.content: A primary key constraint indicates that a column, or group of columns, can be used as a unique identifier for the rows of a table; this requires the values to be both unique and not null.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A table can have at most one primary key, and a primary key can span more than one column (a composite key, composed of two or more attributes). Entity integrity requires that every table have a primary key, and that neither the primary key nor any part of it contain null values.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
A table has at most one primary key, but that key can span multiple columns. Imagine a separate table of branch-specific order numbers in which order number 7 occurs at both North and South branches. The pair BranchCode and OrderNumber can form a composite key if every pair is unique and neither part is null. One key composed of two attributes is not two primary keys.

Check the sample rows deliberately. Duplicate CustomerID values violate the uniqueness requirement. A missing CustomerID violates the not-null requirement. For a composite key, check the combination for uniqueness and every component for null values. A row with a known branch but a null order number does not meet entity integrity.

The practical result is identifying the column or column group that can uniquely identify a row while meeting the stated integrity conditions. A convenient-looking label is not enough: the actual values must satisfy uniqueness and non-null requirements.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Unique is not the whole primary-key rule: values must also be not null, and no part of a composite primary key may be null. A composite key is one primary key spanning columns, not permission to assign several primary keys to a table.

video_need.reason: Checking rows for duplicate and null single-column or composite identifiers makes the integrity requirements visible.

teaching_notes: Distinguish candidate examples from declared keys; avoid CREATE TABLE syntax.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine Customer has primary-key values 101 and 102. Order contains CustomerID to refer to a customer. An order with CustomerID 101 has a matching referenced row; a non-null CustomerID 999 does not in this hypothetical data.

teaching_blocks.title: Foreign Keys Referential Integrity
teaching_blocks.content: A foreign key constraint specifies that the values in a column (or group of columns) of one table must match values appearing in some row of another, referenced table.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A null foreign key value also satisfies referential integrity; a non-null one must match an existing primary key value in the referenced table. A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record; referential integrity is what prevents these.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
The foreign-key constraint requires non-null referencing values to match a value in the referenced table. A row with 999 would be an orphan record if that value is absent from Customer. Referential integrity prevents that unmatched reference rather than making up a new customer to satisfy it.

A null foreign-key value also satisfies referential integrity under this referential-integrity rule. That is different from primary-key rules, where null is not allowed. For the exercise, distinguish three cases: matching 101, unmatched non-null 999, and null. Do not describe all three as simply “valid customer values”: null represents no known referenced value here, while 101 matches an existing customer.

A foreign key can also use a group of columns when the reference requires it. The learner’s immediate task is to check whether the referencing value or values match the required referenced row, while preserving the stated null exception. Keep the example about references and integrity rather than adding deletion or update behavior that has not been established.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: The foreign-key null rule differs from the primary-key rule. In this brief, null satisfies referential integrity; a non-null value must match. Do not treat an unmatched non-null value as an acceptable unknown.

video_need.reason: Tracing matching, null, and orphan references across two small tables clarifies referential integrity.

teaching_notes: Do not invent cascade behavior or NULL prohibitions beyond the brief.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose Customer has one row for customer 101 and one for customer 102. Order has three rows referencing 101 and no rows referencing 102. One customer can therefore relate to many orders, while the example allows a customer to have zero orders.

teaching_blocks.title: One To Many
teaching_blocks.content: In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship, one row on the 'one' side relates to many rows on the 'many' side; for example, one department has many employees.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: In the Customer/Order example, a customer can place a minimum of zero and a maximum of many orders, while an order relates to a maximum of one customer, so Order is the 'many' side (the many side is optional, since a customer doesn't need to place an order to be a customer); the foreign key CustID is placed in the Order table and must match a valid CustID in the Customer table.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Identify Order as the many side. Its CustID foreign key stores the reference to a valid Customer CustID. The same customer identifier can appear on multiple order rows because those rows are different orders belonging to the same customer. The Customer side has the customer row being referenced.

Read the allowed counts in both directions. Customer 101 has several orders; customer 102 has none and still exists as a customer. Each order relates to a maximum of one customer in the stated example. Do not reverse the relationship merely because the customer name is shown on an order report.

The useful modeling decision is not just naming “one-to-many.” It is identifying which thing can have many related instances and placing the reference on that many side. The zero-order customer also shows why “many” should not be interpreted as requiring at least one order in this example. These counts are the business rules of the Customer/Order example, not universal counts for every relationship.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: One-to-many does not mean every one-side row already has several related rows. The stated customer example permits zero orders. Nor should the foreign key be placed on Customer just because that is the one side: CustID belongs in Order for this relationship.

video_need.reason: Linking one customer to several orders and another to none makes direction, optionality, and foreign-key placement visible.

teaching_notes: Preserve the zero-to-many customer example and maximum-one wording for an order.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine orders can include several products, and a product can appear in several orders. That is a many-to-many relationship. In the relational model described here, resolve it using a junction table rather than attempting to implement the many-to-many relationship directly.

teaching_blocks.title: Many To Many Junction Tables
teaching_blocks.content: A many-to-many (M:N) relationship cannot be implemented directly in the relational model; it is resolved into two one-to-many relationships using a composite entity, also called a junction or bridge table.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The junction table must contain at least the primary keys of the two original tables, used as foreign keys, and may also contain additional attributes of its own. The combination of the two original tables' primary keys, brought in as foreign keys, will make the primary key of the junction table (or, together with another attribute, can form it).

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical model, create OrderProduct between Order and Product. It contains OrderID and ProductID, brought in from the original primary keys and used as foreign keys. It may also contain its own attribute, such as quantity. The two original tables now each have a one-to-many relationship with OrderProduct.

Example junction rows are (Order 10, Product A, quantity 2), (Order 10, Product B, quantity 1), and (Order 11, Product A, quantity 3). Order 10 links to two products, and Product A links to two orders. The pair of original identifiers forms the junction primary key in this example. Where needed, those identifiers together with another attribute can form the key.

The important change is the representation of each association as a junction row. Quantity describes that association here, not every occurrence of Product A in every order. Keep both original references visible so the model does not lose one side of the relationship when resolving it.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A junction table is not simply a copy of one original table. It contains at least both original primary keys as foreign keys, and its key uses their combination or that combination with another attribute. Resolving M:N produces two 1:M relationships.

video_need.reason: Transforming a many-to-many association into junction rows and two one-to-many links makes the resolution understandable.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce alternative surrogate-key designs beyond this brief.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose business rules say a customer may have zero or many orders, while each order must relate to exactly one customer. Cardinality expresses permitted counts, not merely the number of rows currently in a sample.

teaching_blocks.title: Relationships and Cardinality
teaching_blocks.content: Relationship cardinality expresses how many instances on either side can be related.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A one-to-many relationship has a column with unique values on one side and potentially repeated matching values on the other. A many-to-many relationship permits repeated matching values on both sides. Determine the relationship by checking whether each side permits one or multiple matching instances. In crow’s-foot notation, a circle (ring) represents zero, a bar (dash) represents one, and a crow’s-foot represents many. Pair a circle and bar for optional zero-or-one, two bars for mandatory exactly-one, a circle and crow’s-foot for optional zero-or-many, or a bar and crow’s-foot for mandatory one-or-many. At each relationship end, place the minimum symbol inward and the maximum symbol closest to the entity box. Draw a relationship line between the entities and annotate both ends with the symbol pair for the number of instances of that end’s entity that can relate to an instance of the other entity.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Check each direction: one customer can match multiple orders, and one order matches one customer. In crow’s-foot notation, place circle plus crow’s-foot at the Order end for zero-or-many orders per customer. Place two bars at the Customer end for mandatory exactly-one customer per order. At each end, put the minimum symbol inward and the maximum symbol closest to the entity box.

The symbols carry separate meanings: circle means zero, bar means one, and crow’s-foot means many. Circle plus bar would mean optional zero-or-one; bar plus crow’s-foot would mean mandatory one-or-many. Use the pair appropriate to the actual business rule instead of choosing whichever shape fits the available space.

The data perspective also helps: one-to-many has unique values on one side and potentially repeated matching values on the other; many-to-many permits repeated matching values on both sides. Determine the relationship by checking whether each side permits one or multiple matching instances. The example’s mandatory order-to-customer rule is a hypothetical business rule for this diagram, not inferred solely from observing one current order.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A relationship end describes how many instances of that end’s entity can relate to an instance of the opposite entity. Reading the crow’s-foot as the count of customers instead of orders reverses the example. A current sample also does not by itself establish all permitted counts.

video_need.reason: Annotating both relationship ends makes crow’s-foot direction, minimum, and maximum counts visible.

teaching_notes: Keep minimum/maximum symbol ordering explicit and do not confuse cardinality with observed row counts.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a business model containing Customer and Order. Draw a named box for each entity and list relevant attributes. For this hypothetical diagram, Customer contains CustomerID and Name; Order contains OrderID, CustomerID, and RequestedDate. Clearly identify CustomerID as Customer’s primary key, OrderID as Order’s primary key, and Order.CustomerID as a foreign key.

teaching_blocks.title: Entity-Relationship Diagrams
teaching_blocks.content: A model diagram can show entity types, their attributes, and relationships between instances.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Draw named entity boxes with relevant attributes, clearly identify primary-key and foreign-key attributes, and connect related entities through each foreign key and its referenced key, marking the permitted multiplicities. Use multiplicity labels such as 1, 0..1, 0..*, or 1..* to state the permitted numbers of related instances.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Connect the foreign-key attribute to its referenced key. Mark permitted multiplicities on the relationship: suppose every order belongs to exactly one customer and each customer may have zero or many orders. Use 1 at the Customer end and 0..* at the Order end for those rules. A 0..1 label would instead allow zero or one; 1..* would require one or many.

Read the diagram back in business language. It says which things are described, what properties they have, how their instances relate, and how many related instances are permitted. The links should correspond to the identified keys rather than being arbitrary lines between boxes.

The result is an entity-relationship diagram, not just a list of tables. The particular attributes and mandatory customer rule are invented for this exercise. In actual modeling, use the established domain information and permitted counts rather than borrowing this example’s rules automatically.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Two boxes joined by an unlabeled line do not communicate the full permitted multiplicities. Likewise, identifying keys without connecting a foreign key to its referenced key leaves the intended relationship unclear. Keep both structural links and allowed counts visible.

video_need.reason: Drawing boxes, identifying keys, and labeling relationship ends shows how the diagram communicates a model.

teaching_notes: Avoid tool-specific ERD commands or additional notation not in the facts.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose one model says the business describes customers and their orders, with customer characteristics and an order relationship. It gives a high-level view of the domain rather than a technical database implementation. Classify that as conceptual based on its business focus and abstraction.

teaching_blocks.title: Conceptual vs Logical Data Models
teaching_blocks.content: A conceptual data model is a high-level business view of the domain, describing important entity classes, their characteristics and constraints, and their relationships rather than a technical database implementation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A logical data model is a less abstract, implementation-independent view that details entities and relationships and their attributes, including attribute data types and lengths. Logical models can specify identifying keys: Oracle Data Modeler allows a primary unique identifier composed of attributes to identify an entity occurrence and foreign unique identifiers that refer to identifiers in another entity. Classify a high-level business-domain overview as conceptual and a more detailed structure with typed attributes, identifiers, and specified relationships as logical, using its level of detail and implementation independence as evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Another model details the attributes, including data types and lengths, identifiers, and specified relationships. Classify that as logical when it remains implementation-independent. For example, it might identify CustomerID as an entity identifier and give Name a text type and stated length. In Oracle Data Modeler, a primary unique identifier can be composed of attributes, and foreign unique identifiers refer to identifiers of another entity.

The distinction rests on level of detail, not on whether the model contains business words. Both can describe the same domain. A conceptual overview emphasizes important entity classes, characteristics, constraints, and relationships; a logical model supplies a less abstract structure without being a technical database implementation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Logical does not mean a specific implemented database. Both classifications here are distinct from technical implementation. Use the detail and implementation independence as evidence, not the drawing’s title alone.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not expand to physical modeling or vendor implementation rules.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a stakeholder asks, “Which customer placed each order, and which requested delivery dates belong to those orders?” Translate that information need into the entities and attributes that can supply it.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Information Needs Mapping
teaching_blocks.content: Business entities and their descriptive attributes give a model the information used to describe a business domain.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Identify the reporting or filtering information needed and match each item to the entity attributes that can supply it.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
In this hypothetical domain, Customer.Name supplies the customer description, Order.RequestedDate supplies the requested date, and the established customer-order relationship connects the two. If the stakeholder wants to filter by branch, look for the entity attribute that actually records branch. If none has been identified, do not pretend the information is available just because the report needs it.

Record a mapping such as “customer name → Customer.Name” and “requested delivery date → Order.RequestedDate.” This makes the relationship between the reporting or filtering request and modeled information explicit. The mapping is conceptual work here; it does not require writing SQL or opening a dashboard tool.

The practical output is a supported account of which attributes provide the requested business information. A stakeholder phrase and an attribute name need not be identical, so explain the match in plain language. Conversely, matching words alone is not enough if the attribute describes something else. Keep the business question visible while checking the model’s entities and descriptive attributes.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Wanting a report does not establish that all needed attributes exist. Match each reporting or filtering need to attributes that can supply it; do not silently invent missing information or introduce query syntax before it is taught.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Stay at needs-to-attributes mapping, not SQL or BI authoring.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the business keeps Customer data and Order data. In the relational model, each named table holds rows of related values. A Customer row could contain one customer’s identifier, name, and contact information; its columns are the fields or attributes describing that kind of thing.

teaching_blocks.title: Relational Model
teaching_blocks.content: A relation, also called a table, holds data where each row (also called a record or tuple) represents one group of related data values.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The columns of a table are also called fields or attributes. A table has a name distinct from every other table in the database, contains no duplicate rows, and the sequence of its rows and columns is insignificant. A database is composed of multiple tables, each holding data. Each table should contain information about one kind of thing only, such as the Branch or the Customer, rather than mixing unrelated things in one table.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
An Order table has its own distinct name and holds order data. Together, multiple tables compose the database. Keep each table about one kind of thing rather than mixing unrelated customer and vehicle descriptions in an arbitrary row.

The relation has no duplicate rows, and the sequence of rows and columns is insignificant to its relational meaning. If two customer rows are displayed in a different order, the display position is not itself a customer attribute. Do not use “the third row” as the business identity of a customer.

The useful mental model is a named table with meaningful fields and related values in each record, within a database of multiple tables. The sample values are hypothetical and the treatment is the relational model. The model describes the data structure, not every behavior a database product may permit. First be able to identify a table, row, and column in the business data.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A row is a group of related data values, not an arbitrary bundle of unrelated things. Table position is also not relational meaning: row and column sequence is insignificant. Keep the relational model distinct from assumptions about how a tool happens to display data.

video_need.reason: A small labeled table is sufficient to distinguish records and fields without a motion demonstration.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce SQL commands or claim every SQL product forbids duplicate stored rows.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose Orders has columns OrderID, CustomerID, and Amount, and a stakeholder needs only identifiers and amounts. SELECT lets you name the desired output columns without asking for every field in the table.

teaching_blocks.title: SQL SELECT Statements
teaching_blocks.content: SELECT retrieves data from a table; the select list names the desired output columns.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write SELECT column1, column2, column3 FROM table_name; to retrieve the named columns. SELECT * FROM table_name; retrieves all columns.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a hypothetical table with rows (10, 101, 40) and (11, 102, 60), write:
SELECT OrderID, Amount FROM Orders;

The output contains OrderID and Amount: the value pairs are (10, 40) and (11, 60). CustomerID was not named in the select list, so it is not one of the output columns. These pairs describe the result contents, not a promised row order.

If you instead write:
SELECT * FROM Orders;
then the result contains all three columns from this example table. The star means all columns, while the named-column form states which columns you want.

Read the query as a request: retrieve OrderID and Amount from Orders. The SELECT list tells you what data appears in the output; FROM tells you the table being queried. The immediate BA use is retrieving the fields needed for a business question. This example does not yet filter, join, total, or sort the data: keep the distinction between choosing output columns and those later operations clear.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: SELECT * means all columns, not a special calculation or a chosen business subset. Naming two columns chooses those output fields. It does not by itself select particular rows or establish an output order.

video_need.reason: The two simple retrieval forms can be compared in a short annotated text example.

teaching_notes: Teach only SELECT lists and FROM; no filtering, aggregation, aliases, or CREATE TABLE.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine Customers contains (101, North Stores) and (102, South Stores), while Orders contains order 10 for customer 101 and order 11 for customer 999. A report needs an order identifier paired with its matching customer name.

teaching_blocks.title: Inner Join
teaching_blocks.content: For each row of T1, an INNER JOIN produces a joined row for each row of T2 that satisfies the join condition; rows from either table with no match are dropped.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The join condition is written in an ON clause, a boolean expression of the same kind used in a WHERE clause, or as a USING clause when both tables use the same column name. INNER is the default kind of join; writing JOIN alone (without CROSS, LEFT, RIGHT, or FULL) means an INNER JOIN.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write:
SELECT Orders.OrderID, Customers.Name FROM Orders INNER JOIN Customers ON Orders.CustomerID = Customers.CustomerID;

The join condition compares the two customer identifiers. Order 10 matches customer 101, producing (10, North Stores). Order 11 has no matching customer row in this deliberately unmatched reporting example, so it is dropped. Customer 102 has no matching order and is also dropped. The unmatched value illustrates join behavior; it is not a valid foreign-key example under an enforced matching constraint.

An INNER JOIN produces a joined row for every satisfying pair, not simply one result for each input table. If multiple rows on the other side satisfy the condition, each matching pair contributes a joined row. The condition can be expressed with ON, or USING when both tables use the same column name. JOIN by itself, without a different join kind, means INNER JOIN.

The practical reporting question is therefore which matches the condition creates and which rows lack matches. Do that reasoning before assuming the result includes every customer or every order.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An inner join does not preserve unmatched rows. Also, “one match per row” is not its general rule: each satisfying pair produces a joined row. In this sample there is one matching pair, but that is a property of the data, not a universal join limit.

video_need.reason: Tracing pairs across two tables makes matching combinations and dropped unmatched rows visible.

teaching_notes: Avoid outer joins and NULL behavior until their entries; unmatched sample intentionally has no enforced FK.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose Orders contains three hypothetical rows: North with Amount 40, North with Amount 60, and South with Amount 30. A stakeholder asks for total amount per branch, not the original order-level rows.

teaching_blocks.title: SQL Aggregation and GROUP BY
teaching_blocks.content: GROUP BY creates one result group for rows with the same grouping-column values.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: SUM computes a total. Write SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) FROM table_name GROUP BY group_column; for one total per group. In the ordinary grouping pattern, list each selected column outside aggregate functions in GROUP BY.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write:
SELECT Branch, SUM(Amount) FROM Orders GROUP BY Branch;

GROUP BY gathers rows with the same Branch value into one result group. SUM computes the total within each group. North contributes 40 + 60 = 100, and South contributes 30. The result contents are therefore (North, 100) and (South, 30), with no output order promised by this query.

In the ordinary grouping pattern, each selected column outside an aggregate function belongs in GROUP BY. Branch is the unaggregated selected column here, while Amount is inside SUM. If the required question changes to totals per branch and service category, the grouping needs to reflect those selected grouping columns rather than pretending one branch total also identifies a single category.

The practical change is the level of the result: several source rows can contribute to one grouped total. Explain that to a stakeholder who expects to see individual orders. The query is not deleting those source details; its requested output is a group-level summary.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Selecting a group label and a total does not make every other source field meaningful at the group level. Follow the ordinary pattern of listing selected nonaggregate columns in GROUP BY. Also distinguish a per-group total from one original row’s amount.

video_need.reason: Gathering repeated branch values into groups and adding amounts makes the change in result level visible.

teaching_notes: Stay with SUM and ordinary grouping; do not introduce other aggregates or vendor exceptions.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine Orders has North amounts 40, 60, and -10, and South amount 30. The business question is “Which branches have more than 90 in positive order amounts?” It contains a row-level condition and a group-level condition.

teaching_blocks.title: SQL Filtering with WHERE and HAVING
teaching_blocks.content: WHERE selects input rows before grouping and aggregate calculation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: HAVING selects groups after grouping and aggregate calculation. Use SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) FROM table_name WHERE row_condition GROUP BY group_column HAVING SUM(value_column) > threshold; to apply both kinds of filtering. In comparisons, = means equal, <> means not equal, and < or > means less or greater than.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write:
SELECT Branch, SUM(Amount) FROM Orders WHERE Amount > 0 GROUP BY Branch HAVING SUM(Amount) > 90;

WHERE retains input rows with positive Amount before grouping. North’s -10 row is excluded, leaving 40 and 60; South’s 30 remains. GROUP BY then creates branch groups and SUM gives North 100 and South 30. HAVING retains groups whose total exceeds 90, leaving North with 100.

The order of those roles matters. The positive-amount condition applies to each input row, while the more-than-90 condition applies to the calculated group total. Describing both as simply “filters” hides that distinction.

The comparison operators express the tests: = means equal, <> not equal, and < or > less or greater than. In this example, > 90 excludes a total equal to 90. Keep the query connected to the business question so the learner can tell which condition belongs before grouping and which belongs afterward.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: WHERE does not filter already-calculated groups in this pattern, and HAVING is not a substitute for the positive-row condition. Filtering inputs can change totals; filtering groups decides which calculated totals remain. An amount threshold and a total threshold are different requirements.

video_need.reason: A staged row-filter, group-total, and group-filter demonstration reveals how each condition changes the result.

teaching_notes: Keep the supported WHERE → grouping → HAVING ordering explicit.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose Orders has Amount values 40, NULL, and 0. The missing value is unknown; it is not the same as a known zero. SQL types also distinguish categories such as integer identifiers, exact monetary values, text, dates, and Boolean values. Choose types whose categories and ranges fit what the business stores.

teaching_blocks.title: SQL Data Types and NULL Handling
teaching_blocks.content: SQL column types distinguish integers, exact numeric values, text, dates, and Boolean values, among other types.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose a column type whose value category and range fit the information being stored. NULL represents an unknown value, and ordinary comparisons with NULL yield unknown rather than true or false. Use WHERE column_name IS NULL or WHERE column_name IS NOT NULL to test for missing values rather than = NULL. COALESCE(value, replacement) returns the first non-NULL argument; use it in the SELECT list to substitute for a missing value. WHERE retains only rows whose condition is true, so unknown results from NULL comparisons do not pass its filter.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
To retrieve the missing-amount rows, use:
SELECT OrderID, Amount FROM Orders WHERE Amount IS NULL;
For known amounts, use IS NOT NULL instead. Do not replace that test with = NULL. Ordinary comparisons involving NULL yield unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows whose condition is true.

For a display that explicitly substitutes zero when Amount is missing, write:
SELECT OrderID, COALESCE(Amount, 0) FROM Orders;
With sample rows (10, 40), (11, NULL), and (12, 0), the displayed pairs are (10, 40), (11, 0), and (12, 0). COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument. The display choice does not prove the original unknown amount was truly zero.

Likewise, WHERE Amount > 0 keeps the 40 row, not the NULL row or the zero row. The NULL comparison is unknown rather than false or true, and unknown does not pass WHERE. Preserving that distinction matters when interpreting what a reporting filter excluded.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: NULL is an unknown value, not automatically zero or empty text. A substitution in SELECT changes the returned display value, not the business meaning of the missing source value. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL for missing-value tests rather than ordinary equality.

video_need.reason: Comparing NULL, zero, tests, and substituted outputs makes missing-value behavior concrete.

teaching_notes: Avoid complete type catalogues or unintroduced casts; retain unknown-versus-zero distinction.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose Customers contains (101, North Stores) and (102, South Stores). Orders contains (10, 101) and (11, 101). The reporting question is “List all customers, with their orders where any match.” Put Customers on the left so that unmatched customer rows are preserved.

teaching_blocks.title: Left Outer Join
teaching_blocks.content: LEFT OUTER JOIN returns matching combinations and preserves each unmatched left-table row.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: For an unmatched left row, columns from the right table are filled with NULL. Write SELECT a.column_name, b.column_name FROM table_a AS a LEFT OUTER JOIN table_b AS b ON a.key_column = b.key_column; with the table to preserve on the left.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write:
SELECT a.CustomerID, b.OrderID FROM Customers AS a LEFT OUTER JOIN Orders AS b ON a.CustomerID = b.CustomerID;

Customer 101 has two matches, producing (101, 10) and (101, 11). Customer 102 has no matching order, so it still appears, with NULL for the right-table OrderID: (102, NULL). Here a and b are the table aliases used in the supplied join pattern.

The result combines matching rows and a preserved unmatched left row. It is not limited to one output row per customer: multiple matching orders produce multiple combinations. NULL in the unmatched row represents the missing right-side fields, not an order identifier equal to zero.

The important decision is which table must remain represented when there is no match. In this example that is Customers. Reversing the table placement without changing the intended join would change which side is guaranteed preservation, so read the FROM and LEFT OUTER JOIN sides together with the business question.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: “Left” refers to table placement in the query, not business importance. A left outer join preserves unmatched left rows and supplies NULL right fields for them. It still returns matching combinations rather than collapsing all matches into one row.

video_need.reason: Showing a customer with two orders and one with none demonstrates matching combinations and left preservation.

teaching_notes: Keep table-preservation logic central; do not introduce reporting totals or distinct-row syntax.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Use a hypothetical report where Orders contains (10, 101) and (11, 101), and Customers contains (101, North Stores) and (102, South Stores). You want all customers represented even if a customer has no orders. With Customers placed on the right, a right outer join preserves that side.

teaching_blocks.title: Right Outer Join
teaching_blocks.content: RIGHT OUTER JOIN returns matching combinations and preserves each unmatched right-table row.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: For an unmatched right row, columns from the left table are filled with NULL. Write SELECT a.column_name, b.column_name FROM table_a AS a RIGHT OUTER JOIN table_b AS b ON a.key_column = b.key_column; with the table to preserve on the right.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write:
SELECT a.OrderID, b.CustomerID FROM Orders AS a RIGHT OUTER JOIN Customers AS b ON a.CustomerID = b.CustomerID;

The matching results include (10, 101) and (11, 101). Customer 102 has no matching order, so the result also includes (NULL, 102). The missing values are from the left table, Orders, because this is an unmatched right-table row.

Compare table position with result interpretation. It is Customers that must remain represented for this business question, and Customers is on the right of RIGHT OUTER JOIN. The join returns matching combinations as well as preserved unmatched right rows. It does not imply that every right row has a real order.

The practical skill is choosing and reading preservation correctly. A report reader seeing NULL for OrderID should understand that the preserved customer lacked a matching left-table row under this condition. Do not turn that missing match into a fabricated order number.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Right outer join preservation follows the right-hand table in the query. For an unmatched right row, left-table fields are NULL. That is the opposite missing-side placement from an unmatched left row in a left outer join.

video_need.reason: Tracing the preserved right side makes unmatched right rows and NULL left fields unmistakable.

teaching_notes: Do not describe right preservation as preserving the first FROM table.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine comparing two independently supplied extracts, rather than tables with an enforced foreign-key relationship. Orders contains (10, 101) and (11, 999); Customers contains (101, North Stores) and (102, South Stores). You want matching combinations plus unmatched rows from either extract.

teaching_blocks.title: Full Outer Join
teaching_blocks.content: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matching combinations and preserves unmatched rows from both tables.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Columns on the missing side of an unmatched row are filled with NULL. Write SELECT a.column_name, b.column_name FROM table_a AS a FULL OUTER JOIN table_b AS b ON a.key_column = b.key_column; to preserve unmatched rows on either side.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write:
SELECT a.OrderID, b.CustomerID FROM Orders AS a FULL OUTER JOIN Customers AS b ON a.CustomerID = b.CustomerID;

The matching pair produces (10, 101). Order 11 has no customer match, so it produces (11, NULL). Customer 102 has no order match, so it produces (NULL, 102). These are result contents, not a guaranteed sequence.

For each unmatched row, fields on the missing side are filled with NULL. The join therefore preserves unmatched rows from both tables instead of choosing only the left or the right side. The sample’s unmatched identifier is deliberate reporting data; it would not satisfy a matching foreign-key constraint.

The business interpretation is that both extracts remain represented under the chosen condition, including rows needing further investigation. A full outer join does not itself repair unmatched references, infer missing customer details, or declare every preserved row valid. Its supported role here is returning matching combinations and preserving unmatched rows from either side.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Preserving unmatched rows is not the same as resolving their missing match. Full outer join supplies NULL for fields from the absent side; it does not invent that side’s data. Matching combinations still appear alongside the unmatched rows.

video_need.reason: Showing one match and unmatched rows from both sides illustrates full preservation and missing-side NULLs.

teaching_notes: Use independent extracts for deliberate unmatched identifiers; do not imply valid FK orphans.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a reporting result contains North amount 100, South amount 100, and West amount 30. Without ORDER BY, its output order is unspecified. A stakeholder’s expectation that the biggest amounts appear first must be stated in the query.

teaching_blocks.title: SQL Sorting and Ordering Results
teaching_blocks.content: Without ORDER BY, a query’s output order is unspecified.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: ORDER BY column ASC sorts ascending and ORDER BY column DESC sorts descending; ASC is the default. Write ORDER BY first_column ASC, second_column DESC to sort by the first column and break its ties with the second. When not otherwise specified, NULL values sort last for ASC and first for DESC; NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST overrides that placement.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write:
SELECT Branch, Amount FROM ReportRows ORDER BY Amount DESC, Branch ASC;

Amount DESC puts larger amounts first. Branch ASC breaks the 100 tie, so the example order is North, South, West. The second sort column matters only when the first values tie. ASC is the default when a direction is omitted.

For the SQL NULL-ordering convention used here, NULL values sort last with ASC and first with DESC unless overridden. To place missing amounts last in a descending report, use:
SELECT Branch, Amount FROM ReportRows ORDER BY Amount DESC NULLS LAST, Branch ASC;

If an East row has NULL Amount, that explicit placement puts it after the non-NULL amounts. Treat the stated default as the documented SQL behavior used here, not a universal assertion about every database engine.

The practical result is an ordering rule a report reader can understand: primary comparison, direction, tie-breaker, and where missing values belong. A consistent-looking order in one earlier result is not a substitute for specifying it.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Observed output order is not a guarantee without ORDER BY. Also, descending does not automatically put NULL last under the documented default here. State NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST when the report needs explicit placement.

video_need.reason: Sorting equal values with a tie-breaker and moving NULL placement makes ordering rules concrete.

teaching_notes: NULL defaults are source/dialect-specific; do not generalize them to all SQL engines.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Reporting Query Patterns
teaching_blocks.content: For a top-N report, compute the metric per group, order it descending, and limit the output: SELECT group_column, SUM(value_column) AS total FROM table_name GROUP BY group_column ORDER BY total DESC, group_column LIMIT n;

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A predictable limited result requires an ordering that determines which rows come first. LAG(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column) retrieves the previous row’s metric for an ordered period comparison; the first row has NULL by default. SUM(metric) OVER (ORDER BY period_column ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) computes an ordered running total over the rows through the current row.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: LIMIT alone does not determine which rows come first. LAG retrieves the previous ordered row, while the specified SUM frame accumulates rows through the current one. Do not describe these distinct calculations as if they all simply return a grouped total.

video_need.reason: Running ranked, previous-row, and cumulative queries against small tables makes their different result states visible.

teaching_notes: Use unique ordered periods in examples; explain only the supplied window patterns.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine receiving a dispatch-orders source with OrderID, Amount, and an unnecessary note column. You need to connect and shape the data before loading it into Power BI Desktop, and Amount should have a type appropriate to its numeric information.

teaching_blocks.title: Power BI Data Import and Transformation
teaching_blocks.content: In Power BI Desktop, Home > Get data selects a connector and connects to a data source.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose Transform Data to open Power Query Editor and shape the data before loading it. Change a column’s data type and remove unnecessary columns using the editor’s column commands; the transformations are recorded as applied steps. Use Close & Apply to apply the transformations and load the shaped data.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Use Home > Get data to select the connector and connect to the source. Choose Transform Data to open Power Query Editor. There, use column commands to change Amount’s data type and remove the note column that is unnecessary for this example. The transformations are recorded as applied steps.

Inspect the intended shape before loading: the example needs the order identifier and amount, with the correct type for Amount. The applied steps record the transformations rather than requiring you to describe them only from memory. Then use Close & Apply to apply the changes and load the shaped data.

The practical distinction is between connecting to a source and shaping the data before loading. The path teaches tool use from scratch, so keep the connector, editor, and final apply action explicit. This example does not yet create relationships, measures, or report visuals. Its output is loaded, shaped data for later work, not a completed dashboard merely because a connection succeeded.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Get data is the connection step, not the whole transformation workflow. Transform Data opens the editor, and Close & Apply applies and loads the shaped result. Recorded applied steps are transformations, not a substitute for checking the intended columns and types.

video_need.reason: The connector, Power Query column commands, applied steps, and Close & Apply are best understood as a tool workflow.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce DAX, BI relationships, or report canvas commands.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a hypothetical Tableau report needs Customers and Orders from a source. Start in the Connect pane, choose the appropriate connector, and provide that source’s connection information. Connection details depend on the selected source.

teaching_blocks.title: Tableau Data Connection and Preparation
teaching_blocks.content: Select a connector in Tableau’s Connect pane and provide the source-specific connection information.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: To create a physical join, drag the first table to the canvas, double-click it, then drag another table into that join canvas. Select the join type and matching fields in the join dialog; inner keeps matches, left or right preserves its named side, and full outer preserves both sides. An extract is a saved snapshot of data for analysis; select Extract on the Data Source page and configure the extract before saving it.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a physical join, drag the first table to the canvas, double-click it, and then drag the second table into the join canvas. In the join dialog, choose the join type and matching fields. If the question requires all customers, place and preserve the named side appropriately; inner keeps matches, left or right preserves its named side, and full outer preserves both.

If the workflow uses an extract, select Extract on the Data Source page and configure it before saving. An extract is a saved snapshot for analysis, not a claim that it always shows the newest source state.

The useful output is a connection and prepared data arrangement suited to the reporting question. Keep the physical-join canvas step explicit: dragging tables without explaining the double-click entry to that canvas leaves a beginner without the named workflow. The example ends at preparation, not at worksheet charts or dashboard placement.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: An extract is a saved snapshot, so do not describe it as inherently live. Also preserve the distinction between connecting, creating a physical join in its canvas, and selecting an extract. Those are different preparation choices and actions.

video_need.reason: Navigating Connect, the physical-join canvas, the join dialog, and Extract benefits from an annotated tool demonstration.

teaching_notes: Avoid conflating physical joins with logical relationship modeling.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an operations team wants to improve dispatch preparation. Before defining the desired result, record the present situation as a baseline. In this hypothetical assessment, dispatch information is kept in separate records, clarification calls occur before preparation, and one branch uses a different handoff from another.

teaching_blocks.title: Current-State Capability Assessment
teaching_blocks.content: A current-state assessment describes the present situation as a baseline for identifying improvements.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Record detailed notes about the current business situation in a structured current-state column. Organize the current-state notes by the business areas being assessed so they can be compared with goals and gaps.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Put detailed current-state notes in a structured current-state column. Organize them by business area: instruction access, handoffs, and dispatch preparation. That organization makes later comparison possible without mixing every observation into one vague statement such as “the process is inefficient.”

For instruction access, the example note might be “Staff consult a separate sheet for current instructions.” For handoffs, it might describe who supplies amended information. If the scenario provides a measured preparation time, record it with its context. Do not invent a baseline number merely because a later target will need comparison.

The output is a description of the present business situation arranged by the areas being assessed. It is not yet a list of desired changes. Keep an observed condition, a proposed improvement, and a judgment about success separate. This way a reader can see what current situation the subsequent goals and gaps refer to, rather than having to reconstruct the baseline from the recommendation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Current-state assessment is not a wish list. A note saying “use one instruction record” describes a desired change, not the current situation. Record the baseline in the current-state column and organize it by the assessed business areas.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Stay with structured baseline notes; do not assume measurements absent from the situation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the current-state assessment records lengthy dispatch preparation and unclear instruction access. Future-state vision states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve, with a business outcome and measurable success target.

teaching_blocks.title: Future-State Vision Definition
teaching_blocks.content: A desired-state definition states the objectives and situation the business wants to achieve.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Express the goal using a business outcome and measurable success target. Write the desired objectives alongside the corresponding business areas in the desired-state column.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical effort, a desired objective could be “Dispatch staff prepare orders with current instructions, with preparation completed within five minutes in the stated operating conditions.” The five-minute target is an example business decision, not a standard for every dispatch operation. It gives the desired state more substance than “make dispatch better.”

Write desired objectives in the desired-state column beside the corresponding business areas. The instruction-access objective belongs alongside the instruction-access baseline; the preparation target belongs alongside the preparation baseline. Keeping that alignment visible lets readers compare like areas rather than comparing a broad aspiration with an unrelated current note.

The useful output is a future situation described in terms of business outcome and success target. It does not need to name a particular tool as the vision. “Purchase software” states an action, while “staff have current instructions and meet the preparation target” describes what the business wants to achieve. Keep the target’s conditions visible so its meaning is not lost in a slogan.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A future-state vision is not merely a named solution or a favorable adjective. State the desired business outcome with a measurable success target. It is intended future behavior, not evidence that the business has already reached that state.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not turn the desired target into an unsupported universal service level.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the current-state column says dispatch preparation takes twelve minutes under the assessed conditions, while the desired-state column sets a five-minute target under the same conditions. The specific time difference is seven minutes. Another current note says staff consult two instruction sources, while the desired state calls for current instructions available in one place.

teaching_blocks.title: Gap Identification and Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: A gap is a specific difference between the current situation and the desired state.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Compare the current-state description with the desired-state objectives and list the specific differences keeping the business from those goals.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Compare each current description with its corresponding desired objective. List the specific differences keeping the business from the goal: the preparation-time difference and the information-access difference in this hypothetical case. These are more precise than writing only “there is a dispatch gap.”

Keep the comparison tied to the descriptions supplied. If the current-state record contains no preparation-time measurement, do not calculate a numerical difference by inventing one. You can still identify the documented qualitative difference and preserve any missing information as a question.

The output is a gap list grounded in current and desired states. It does not itself prove the cause of every gap or choose the solution. The immediate analytical task is to make the difference explicit enough that stakeholders can see what has to change. The example’s numbers and one-place objective illustrate that comparison, not a claim about a real organization.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A gap is the difference between current and desired states, not simply a complaint or a proposed fix. “Buy a new system” does not identify the difference. Compare corresponding descriptions and state what separates the business from its goal.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not infer root causes or guaranteed solutions from a gap alone.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an order-service team is assessing a business situation. Its experienced dispatch staff are an internal advantage, while fragmented instruction records are an internal limitation. A new external delivery partnership may create a favorable possibility, while an external competitor’s improved service may threaten success.

teaching_blocks.title: SWOT Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: SWOT separates strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in a business situation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Strengths are internal advantages; weaknesses are internal limitations. Opportunities are favorable external possibilities; threats are external factors that could harm success. Create four labeled quadrants and place each factor according to whether it is internal or external and favorable or unfavorable.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Create four labeled quadrants: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats. Place experienced staff under Strengths and fragmented records under Weaknesses. Place the partnership possibility under Opportunities and the competitor factor under Threats. These are hypothetical factors selected to make the two distinctions clear.

For each placement, ask two questions: is the factor internal or external, and favorable or unfavorable? Strong staff and the partnership are both favorable, but one is internal and the other external. Fragmentation and the competitor factor are both unfavorable, but they also belong on different sides of that distinction.

The useful result is an organized view of the situation rather than an unclassified list of positive and negative comments. Do not classify solely by whether a factor sounds important. A favorable external possibility belongs under Opportunities even if the team hopes to benefit from it internally. Keep the classification tied to the factor being described.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Strengths and opportunities are not interchangeable synonyms for positives; internal versus external distinguishes them. The same distinction separates weaknesses from threats. A four-quadrant layout helps only when each factor is placed using both dimensions.

video_need.reason: A simple labeled four-quadrant visual is enough; motion would mostly repeat the classifications.

teaching_notes: Avoid scoring SWOT factors or implying SWOT proves causation.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine prioritizing requirements for an initial delivery-instruction release. Define that scope before assigning MoSCoW categories. In this hypothetical scope, seeing current instructions is essential: without it, the solution would not work for its stated purpose, so the group assigns Must have.

teaching_blocks.title: MoSCoW Prioritization
teaching_blocks.content: MoSCoW groups requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have, or Will not have for the scope being prioritized.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Must-have items are essential: without them the solution would not work or the project would be useless. Should-have items are important but the solution can still work without them. Could-have items are desirable but nonessential and have a smaller impact if omitted. Will-not-have items are not needed within the prioritization scope and can be deprioritized or dropped. Define the prioritization scope, discuss each item’s importance, and assign the category the group agrees fits it.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
An amendment indicator is important but the solution can still work without it, so it is a Should have in this example. A convenience color choice is desirable, nonessential, and has a smaller omission impact, so it is a Could have. A vehicle-purchasing feature is not needed within this scope, so it is Will not have. The same labels are not universal classifications of those features; they depend on the agreed scope and importance.

Discuss each item’s importance and assign the category the group agrees fits. Keep the reasoning attached to the category so Must have is not simply a synonym for “a stakeholder wants it strongly.” Should have and Could have both allow a working solution without the item, but the described importance and omission impact differ.

The practical output is scope-specific grouping that distinguishes essential work from important, desirable, or excluded work. Will not have refers to what is not needed within the prioritization scope; it need not be rewritten as a claim that the organization must never consider that item.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: MoSCoW categories are not just four levels of enthusiasm. Must have is essential to a working or useful solution in the stated scope. Will not have is scope-specific, not necessarily a permanent ban. Define the scope and discuss importance before assigning labels.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Keep “Will not have” terminology from the brief; no unsupported percentage allocations.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose user evidence about an order service shows several different satisfaction patterns. Users expect their current instructions to be accurate and are dissatisfied when they are missing; providing them adds little extra satisfaction. That pattern fits a Must-be or basic feature.

teaching_blocks.title: Kano Analysis
