teaching_blocks.content: Kano classifies features by how functionality relates to customer satisfaction.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Must-be or basic features are expected; their absence causes dissatisfaction, while their presence adds little satisfaction. Performance features produce more satisfaction as their functionality improves. Attractive or excitement features can delight users who did not expect them and may not notice their absence. Use user evidence about satisfaction and the feature’s functionality to classify and discuss the appropriate category. Indifferent features are those users feel neutral toward: changes in their functionality do not significantly increase or decrease customer satisfaction.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Evidence might show that progressively quicker instruction access produces more satisfaction: that is a Performance pattern. An unexpected helpful suggestion could delight users while its absence goes unnoticed: that is an Attractive or excitement pattern. If users remain neutral as a feature’s functionality changes, it is Indifferent.

Classify using evidence about satisfaction and functionality, not the BA’s personal excitement about an idea. In this hypothetical case, the same design team might find a decorative feature exciting while user evidence shows neutrality. The evidence would support Indifferent rather than Attractive.

The useful output is a discussion of how functionality relates to satisfaction. These categories do not state delivery priority by themselves. A feature being expected is a satisfaction pattern, while a separate prioritization decision asks what belongs in the delivery scope.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Attractive means it can delight users who did not expect it; it does not mean the team likes the feature. Basic features can cause dissatisfaction when absent even though their presence adds little satisfaction. Preserve that asymmetry instead of treating all features as linear satisfaction gains.

video_need.reason: Contrasting expected, improving, surprising, and neutral satisfaction patterns benefits from visual curves or changing states.

teaching_notes: Include Indifferent; avoid adding unsupported Kano categories or survey procedures.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine comparing two hypothetical instruction-access options on clarity and implementation fit. Assign importance weights 0.6 to clarity and 0.4 to fit. Use a consistent scale where higher scores are better. Option A scores 4 and 2; Option B scores 3 and 4.

teaching_blocks.title: Weighted Scoring Models
teaching_blocks.content: A weighted decision matrix compares options on criteria whose weights represent importance.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: List the criteria and options, assign criterion weights, and score every option against each criterion using a consistent scale. Multiply each criterion score by its weight and add those products for the option’s total weighted score. Compare the totals to rank the options; the highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen criteria and weights.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Multiply each score by its criterion weight and add the products. A totals 4 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.4 = 3.2. B totals 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.4 = 3.4. B ranks higher under these chosen criteria, weights, and scores.

The highest total is typically the best choice under the chosen setup, not a universal fact that B is best in every context. The weights represent importance, and the scores express performance on the consistent scale. Record them so another reader can understand the comparison rather than seeing only the final total.

The practical output is an explicit weighted comparison of options. If a stakeholder challenges the recommendation, return to the criteria, importance weights, and scores. Do not defend 3.4 as if it were independent of those choices. The example weights sum to one; the key calculation is score times weight, summed across criteria.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Adding unweighted scores is not the weighted-total calculation. Multiply each criterion score by its importance weight first. Also keep the qualification: the highest total is typically best under the chosen criteria and weights, not proof of an objectively best solution in all circumstances.

video_need.reason: A worked matrix can show score-by-weight products and how they combine into option totals.

teaching_notes: Preserve “typically”; do not prescribe weight normalization as mandatory.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose stakeholders are choosing between two instruction-access solutions. Define shared criteria before comparing them: instruction clarity and fit with the agreed operating constraints. For this hypothetical assessment, use weights 0.6 and 0.4 and a common score scale.

teaching_blocks.title: Solution Option Evaluation and Recommendation
teaching_blocks.content: Solution comparison uses defined decision criteria rather than an unstructured preference.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Score each candidate solution against the same criteria and multiply the scores by the corresponding importance weights. Sum each candidate’s weighted scores, compare the totals, and explain the recommendation in terms of the criteria and scores.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Solution A scores 4 for clarity and 2 for fit, giving 4 × 0.6 + 2 × 0.4 = 3.2. Solution B scores 3 and 4, giving 3 × 0.6 + 4 × 0.4 = 3.4. Compare the totals and recommend B on this assessment, explaining that its stronger fit outweighs A’s clarity advantage under the selected weights.

The recommendation should point back to the criteria and scores. “We prefer B” omits the analytical basis; “B totals 3.4 under the agreed clarity and fit assessment” makes that basis visible. The two totals are hypothetical and depend on the chosen assessment, not a claim about real products.

The useful BA output is a reasoned solution recommendation, not only a completed matrix. State what was compared, how importance affected the scores, and how the resulting totals support the recommendation. Keep candidate solutions on the same criteria rather than awarding one option points for an advantage the other option was never assessed against.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A preferred option does not become a supported recommendation merely because it is given a score. Evaluate every candidate against the same criteria and weights, calculate the totals, and explain the recommendation in those terms rather than using an unstructured preference.

video_need.reason: A comparison table can link criterion scores, weighted totals, and the reason for a recommendation.

teaching_notes: Avoid claims that scores guarantee implementation success.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a business case for improving delivery-instruction access. Describe the dispatch problem, possible solutions, and expected benefits and costs. For this hypothetical one-year assessment, estimated monetary benefits are 18,000 and relevant project costs total 12,000, including implementation and other relevant costs rather than only a headline purchase price.

teaching_blocks.title: Business Case Development
teaching_blocks.content: A business case justifies an initiative by describing the problem, possible solutions, expected benefits, and costs.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: List and estimate relevant costs and benefits over the period being evaluated, including direct and indirect effects. Present the recommendation with the supporting financial assessment in the business case. For a monetary-return estimate, calculate projected net return = total projected monetary benefits over the evaluation period − project cost, including the cost of the project itself rather than reporting gross savings alone. Interpret a positive projected monetary return as estimated benefits exceeding cost over that period, and report the assumptions and time horizon because the return is an estimate, not a promised financial outcome. Calculate percentage ROI = (monetary benefits − costs) / costs × 100%, using net monetary return as the numerator and investment cost as the denominator. Use the costs and monetary benefits for the stated evaluation period, include relevant costs rather than just a headline purchase cost, and use the same time period when comparing alternatives. Net monetary return is the benefits-minus-costs amount in money, whereas percentage ROI expresses that net return relative to investment cost.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Projected net monetary return is benefits minus costs: 18,000 − 12,000 = 6,000. Percentage ROI is that net return divided by investment cost, times 100%: 6,000 / 12,000 × 100% = 50%. The 6,000 amount and 50% percentage describe different things. Gross benefits of 18,000 are not the net return.

A positive projected monetary return means the estimated benefits exceed cost over the stated period. Report the one-year horizon and the assumptions behind the estimates; this is not a promised financial outcome. If another alternative is compared, use costs and monetary benefits for the same evaluation period, including relevant direct and indirect effects.

Present the recommendation with its supporting financial assessment in the business case. Do not let the calculation replace the problem and option descriptions. The useful output explains why the initiative is being considered and what estimated return supports the recommendation, with the costs, period, and assumptions visible to readers.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: ROI’s numerator is net monetary return, not gross savings. Its denominator is investment cost, not benefits. A positive projection is an estimate under stated assumptions and a time horizon, not a promise. Net return in money and percentage ROI must not be labeled interchangeably.

video_need.reason: Tracing costs and benefits into net return and percentage ROI makes denominators, units, and time horizons clear.

teaching_notes: Keep cost completeness, same-period comparisons, and estimates explicit; no unsupported NPV or payback formulas.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose two instruction-access options differ in cost and clarity. Cost is measured in money, while clarity uses a rating. Adding 8,000 directly to a clarity score of 4 would mix incompatible units, so define a common rating scale first.

teaching_blocks.title: Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis
teaching_blocks.content: A decision matrix enables comparison across several criteria using explicit importance weights and scores.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define criteria and importance weights, then map each criterion’s performance values to a common rating scale with criterion-specific scoring definitions applied consistently to all options and higher ratings meaning better performance. Calculate each option’s total by multiplying its common-scale rating for each criterion by that criterion’s weight and summing these weighted ratings, rather than raw values in incompatible units, then compare totals for a defensible ranking.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical matrix, clarity already uses 1 to 5, with higher ratings better. Define cost ratings specifically: 8,000 maps to 5 and 12,000 maps to 3 for the example options, because lower cost is better under the chosen scoring definitions. Apply each criterion’s definition consistently to every option. Assign weights 0.4 to cost and 0.6 to clarity.

Option A has cost rating 5 and clarity 3, totaling 5 × 0.4 + 3 × 0.6 = 3.8. Option B has cost rating 3 and clarity 5, totaling 3 × 0.4 + 5 × 0.6 = 4.2. Compare those totals for the ranking.

The useful output makes criteria, importance, criterion-specific scoring definitions, and weighted totals explicit. The invented mappings are part of this assessment, not a universal monetary conversion. Higher ratings must mean better performance across the criteria, including cost, so the weighted sum has a consistent interpretation.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Weights do not make incompatible raw units directly comparable. Map performance to a common rating scale with criterion-specific definitions first. Also reverse the scoring direction where needed so higher ratings mean better performance rather than accidentally rewarding higher cost.

video_need.reason: Mapping different units to a common scale before calculating weighted totals benefits from a worked matrix.

teaching_notes: No invented normalization formula; use explicitly defined sample ratings.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine five observed dispatch-preparation times in minutes: 2, 3, 3, 4, and 18. The mean is the sum divided by the number of observations: 30 / 5 = 6 minutes. The ordered middle value is 3, so the median is 3 minutes. The most frequent value is also 3, so the mode is 3 minutes.

teaching_blocks.title: Descriptive Measures Of Center
teaching_blocks.content: The sample mean is computed as the sum of the observed values divided by the number of observations.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The median is the middle value when the data are ordered from smallest to largest; if there is an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle values. The mode is the value that occurs most often in the data; there can be more than one mode. The mean is more strongly affected by extreme observations (such as those in the tail of a skewed distribution) than the median, which is more robust to them; for this reason the median can better represent a typical value in a skewed dataset.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
The extreme 18-minute observation affects the mean more strongly than the median. In this skewed sample, the median can better represent a typical value than the mean. Do not hide the extreme observation; explain why the two center summaries differ.

For an even-sized example, 2, 3, 4, and 9 has median (3 + 4) / 2 = 3.5. For mode, 2, 2, 4, and 4 has two most frequent values, so both 2 and 4 are modes. These examples apply the definitions rather than assuming every dataset has a single mode or a median that is an observed value.

The practical BA task is to interpret a center measure in the context of the business data. A report saying “average preparation time is 6 minutes” should be clear that it uses the mean. The median answers a different center question and is more robust to extreme observations.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Mean, median, and mode are not interchangeable names for one number. Order values before finding the median, average the two middle values when the count is even, and allow multiple modes. An extreme value can pull the mean away from the median.

video_need.reason: Ordering values and changing an extreme observation makes center measures and their sensitivity visible.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce inferential statistics or automatic outlier removal.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose dispatch-preparation times are 2, 4, and 6 minutes. Their mean is 4. The range is 6 − 2 = 4 minutes. For the sample variance, subtract the mean from each observation to get -2, 0, and 2; square these deviations to get 4, 0, and 4; then sum to 8.

teaching_blocks.title: Measures Of Spread
teaching_blocks.content: The range of a data set is the largest value minus the smallest value.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The variance is computed by taking each observation's deviation from the mean, squaring it, summing the squared deviations, and dividing by n - 1 (one less than the number of observations); it is roughly the average squared distance of the observations from the mean. The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, and it describes the typical distance of an observation from the mean. The standard deviation is expressed in the same units as the original data, while the variance is expressed in squared units; the range is based only on the two most extreme values and ignores how the rest of the data are spread.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Divide by n − 1, which is 2 for three observations: variance is 8 / 2 = 4 square minutes. Standard deviation is the square root of that variance, or 2 minutes. The different units matter: variance is squared, while standard deviation uses the original minutes and describes typical distance from the mean.

Range only uses the smallest and largest values. A second sample, 2, 4, 4, 4, and 6, has the same range, but its variance is 8 / 4 = 2 square minutes and standard deviation is about 1.41 minutes. The added central observations change the spread calculation without changing the extremes.

The practical reporting point is that range alone does not describe how the rest of the data are spread. State which measure you use and its units. The variance formula here is the sample form with n − 1; keep that denominator instead of silently switching to another convention.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Do not divide this sample-variance calculation by n: the stated denominator is n − 1. Standard deviation is not the variance itself, and it is not in squared units. Equal ranges also do not prove equal spread among all observations.

video_need.reason: Tracing deviations, squares, denominator, and square root makes the calculation and units concrete.

teaching_notes: Explicitly label sample variance; examples have at least two observations.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a backlog story saying, “As a dispatcher, I want all order-management capabilities, so that I can do my work.” It is broad enough that the team cannot clearly discuss its scope or finish it within an iteration. Refinement breaks oversized items into smaller, more precise stories.

teaching_blocks.title: User Story Writing and Refinement
teaching_blocks.content: A user story states a persona’s need and its purpose using “As a [persona], I [want to], [so that].”

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Refine oversized backlog items by breaking them into smaller, more precise items with clearer descriptions. Split larger stories into smaller stories that can be completed within an iteration. Use INVEST as a quality checklist for each rewritten or split story; if a criterion fails, consider rewording or rewriting the story. Independent means stories should not overlap in concept and should be schedulable and implementable in any order; check whether a story can be implemented without requiring another story first. Negotiable means a story captures the essential need rather than a fixed contract of feature details; check that details can be worked out collaboratively with the customer. Valuable means a story delivers value to the customer; check that each split story describes a customer-valued result rather than only a technical layer. Estimable means the team can approximate the work well enough to rank and schedule it; check that the team understands the story and its scope well enough to make an estimate. Small means a story fits within an iteration; check the size of each proposed story and split work that cannot fit. Testable means the desired result is clear enough to write a test for it; check that the customer can describe how to verify the story, and clarify stories whose result cannot be tested.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical case, rewrite one story around seeing current instructions and another around finding orders by customer. Each needs a persona’s need and purpose, not merely a technical layer. Check each rewritten story with INVEST. Independent asks whether it can be implemented without requiring the other first and without conceptual overlap. Negotiable asks whether it captures the essential need while details remain open to collaboration. Valuable asks whether it delivers a customer-valued result.

Estimable asks whether the team understands it well enough to approximate the work for ranking and scheduling. Small asks whether it fits within an iteration. Testable asks whether the customer can describe how to verify the result. If the rewritten instruction story still says only “make access better,” clarify it until a test can be described. If it cannot fit, split it further.

The output is not just more story cards. It is a set of clearer, smaller stories checked for all six qualities. The example split is a candidate to assess, not a guarantee of independence or size without the team’s checks.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Splitting into “database,” “interface,” and “testing” pieces does not by itself satisfy Valuable: each split story should describe a customer-valued result. Nor does using the story sentence format prove INVEST is met. Check each quality and reword or rewrite failures.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Include all INVEST meanings; do not assume an invented split is automatically independent.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the order-service backlog contains a broad instruction-access item, a clearer customer-search item, and an outdated vague item called “reporting improvements.” The product backlog is an emergent ordered list of needed product-improvement work, not a fixed archive of every initial idea.

teaching_blocks.title: Backlog Management
teaching_blocks.content: A product backlog is an emergent, ordered list of work needed to improve the product.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Refinement breaks items into smaller, more precise items and adds details such as description, order, and size. Review unclear or oversized items, clarify their details, split them as needed, and keep the backlog ordered. Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the needed transparency.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Refine unclear or oversized items. For the instruction item, clarify the description and break it into smaller, more precise items if needed. For the vague reporting item, establish the intended detail before treating it as ready. Add detail such as description, order, and size, then keep the backlog ordered.

Items that can be completed within one iteration are ready for selection; refinement usually provides the transparency needed for that judgment. Do not label an oversized item ready merely because it appears near the top. Conversely, refinement is not just changing order: it also improves detail and precision.

The useful BA contribution is clearer items and an understandable ordered backlog. Keep clarification, splitting, detail, and ordering visible rather than treating the backlog as a static archive.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A backlog is not simply an unordered requirements list. Refinement also does more than re-rank items: it makes them smaller and more precise with relevant details. High placement alone does not establish that an item fits within an iteration.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Preserve “usually” for refinement transparency; avoid assigning later Scrum accountabilities prematurely.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine planned order-service work includes current-instruction access, a customer-search improvement, and broader multi-branch reporting. A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than presenting disconnected features.

teaching_blocks.title: Phased Delivery Sequencing
teaching_blocks.content: A roadmap sequences planned work against goals rather than listing disconnected features.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Group planned initiatives into a sequence such as Now, Next, and Later, linking the sequence to goals and tracking dependencies. Review the sequence as priorities and information change rather than treating the initial roadmap as fixed.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical roadmap, place instruction access in Now to support the dispatch-preparation goal, customer search in Next to support faster order finding, and multi-branch reporting in Later to support branch comparison. Track known dependencies as part of the sequence. If later reporting depends on agreed branch information, make that connection visible instead of treating the three labels as independent wish lists.

Now, Next, and Later are an example sequence, not fixed dates promised by this concept. Link each initiative to its goal so a stakeholder can understand why it occupies that part of the roadmap. Then review the sequence as priorities and information change.

If new information changes which work supports the immediate goal, reconsider the initial placement. The useful output is goal-linked planned sequencing with dependencies and revision, not a permanent commitment disguised as a diagram. The example initiatives are invented for the exercise; their particular order is not a universal rule for BA delivery.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A roadmap is not just a list of features with three headings. The sequence should connect to goals and track dependencies. Also, the initial sequence is not fixed: review it as priorities and information change rather than claiming the first roadmap cannot be revised.

video_need.reason: A goal-linked sequence with dependency cues can make the relationship between initiatives and phases easier to follow.

teaching_notes: Do not invent scheduling authority or fixed durations for Now/Next/Later.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a story says dispatchers want to see current instructions so they can prepare the correct order. Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to judge whether this particular story is satisfied. Discuss what completing it means instead of relying only on the story’s short wording.

teaching_blocks.title: Acceptance Criteria Definition
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria state the conditions used to determine whether a particular user story is satisfied.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Discuss what completing the story means, make the acceptance conditions testable, and document that shared understanding. Refinement adds detail to make backlog items more precise and understandable.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical case, the stakeholders agree that selecting an existing order displays its current instructions, and selecting an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Make those acceptance conditions testable and document the shared understanding. “The lookup is good” does not describe a clear completion condition.

During refinement, add detail that makes the backlog item more precise and understandable. If stakeholders disagree about what “current” means, clarify that point before leaving the criterion as if everyone interpreted it identically. The example conditions are agreed choices for this story, not a complete checklist for all instruction-access systems.

The useful output is story-specific completion understanding that can be checked. It should connect directly to the desired behavior rather than becoming a broad quality slogan. Keep the conditions in the shared record so later discussion is about the documented understanding, not a different person’s recollection of what was meant.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria belong to a particular story. They are not a substitute for clarifying what that story means, and vague positive wording does not make them testable. Discuss and document the shared completion conditions instead of assuming the title is sufficient.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce Definition of Done early; focus on testable story conditions.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine an operations manager receiving a report about dispatch delays. A page of observations alone leaves the reader to find the main conclusion. Structure the report for its readers and purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: Written Business Reports
teaching_blocks.content: A report should be structured for its readers rather than assuming the findings speak for themselves.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Put the key message in headlines for readers who only scan, then provide highlights and supporting detail for readers who need more. Write at the level of detail the audience needs and select information that serves the report’s purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical report, a headline could state “Instruction clarification is the main issue identified in dispatch preparation.” Highlights then summarize the relevant findings, and supporting detail explains the evidence available in the exercise. The headline is an example report conclusion based on assumed findings, not a claim that clarification is always the main delay.

This layering serves different reading needs. A scanning reader can find the key message; a reader needing more can continue into highlights and detail. Select information that serves the report’s purpose and use the audience’s required level of detail rather than including every note simply because it exists.

The practical output is not a shorter report at any cost. It is an organized report whose key message is prominent and whose supporting information remains available. If the purpose is to communicate the dispatch finding, unrelated observations about office equipment distract from that purpose. Keep enough relevant detail for the intended reader without assuming findings will explain themselves.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Supporting detail does not remove the need for a clear key message. Conversely, a headline alone is not the same as a structured report for readers who need evidence. Use headlines, highlights, and relevant detail rather than choosing between a slogan and an unorganized data dump.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_blocks.title: Communicating to Technical vs Non-Technical Audiences
teaching_blocks.content: The audience determines appropriate detail, terminology, and how information is communicated.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use the audience’s language and explain an unfamiliar concept with a familiar analogy when useful. Make the main ideas clear in headlines while preserving supporting detail for readers who need it.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For managers, a headline might say “Missing instruction matches leave some orders unresolved,” followed by the operational meaning. For technical readers familiar with the query, supporting detail can identify the relevant matching fields and the result behavior. Both explanations should preserve the same finding; changing audience is not permission to change the evidence.

Use the audience’s language. If an unfamiliar relationship needs explanation, a familiar analogy may help: a customer identifier can be compared to a reference that points to a customer record. Use the analogy to clarify the concept, not replace its actual meaning. Keep the main ideas clear in headlines and preserve detail for readers who need it.

A nontechnical audience does not require a different conclusion, and a technical audience does not require every possible implementation detail. teaching_blocks.content: Audience adaptation changes detail and language, not the supported facts. Unexplained jargon can obscure the main idea, while deleting all supporting detail can leave readers unable to understand it. Preserve clear headlines and the detail appropriate to their needs.

teaching_blocks.content: A presentation needs a narrative that makes findings meaningful to its audience rather than a bare list of data.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Structure the presentation around clear headlines, highlights, and supporting detail appropriate to different reader needs. Use audience-appropriate language and connect findings to the recommendation being communicated.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical presentation, the opening headline states the dispatch problem, the next highlight explains the relevant instruction-access finding, and the recommendation follows with its supporting detail. The exact sequence is an example structure, not a compulsory slide count. Use audience-appropriate language to connect the finding to what you recommend.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose delivery-instruction requirements are ready for stakeholder review. Plan the walkthrough around the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions. teaching_blocks.content: Requirements review gives stakeholders and approvers the opportunity to confirm priorities and agree what will be delivered.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Plan a review around the documented goal, scope, requirements, assumptions, and open questions. Record decisions in the shared requirements document so agreement and unresolved questions remain visible. Close the walkthrough agenda by asking designated approvers to approve the reviewed requirements or state outstanding conditions, and record the approval outcome, approvers, and any unresolved conditions in the shared decision log.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
In this hypothetical walkthrough, review the instruction-display requirement and its acceptance conditions, then make the unresolved meaning of “current” visible. Record decisions in the shared requirements document instead of letting meeting discussion become the only source of agreement.

Close the agenda by asking designated approvers to approve the reviewed requirements or state outstanding conditions. Record the approval outcome, the approvers, and any unresolved conditions in the shared decision log. For example, the record might state that approval remains conditional on clarifying the instruction-update rule. That is different from recording unconditional approval.

The useful output is a visible agreement and decision record. A demonstration can support discussion, but the fact that a feature was shown does not itself record approval. Keep the reviewed scope and unresolved questions connected to the decision so later readers can understand what was actually agreed and what remains open.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Attendance or a successful demonstration is not an approval record. Ask designated approvers for approval or outstanding conditions, then record the outcome and approvers. Do not rewrite a conditional outcome as full agreement merely because the walkthrough ended.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine defining the boundary of an order service. A context diagram represents the system as a single central element, with external entities outside its boundary. The immediate question is what is inside this system and what exchanges information with it.

teaching_blocks.title: Scope Modeling / Context Diagrams
teaching_blocks.content: A context diagram represents the system as a single element with a boundary separating it from external entities.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Define the system’s purpose and boundary and identify its external actors and connected systems. Draw the system centrally, place external entities around it, and use labeled directional arrows to show exchanges.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical diagram, draw “Order service” centrally. Place “Dispatcher” and “External delivery service” around it as external entities. Label directional arrows with the exchanges: a dispatcher sends an order-selection request to the system; the system returns instructions; the system sends a dispatch request to the delivery service. These are example exchanges, not mandatory integrations.

Define the system’s purpose and boundary before placing the entities. Do not put the external delivery service inside merely because it communicates with the order service. The directional labels help the reader distinguish what flows into and out of the central system.

The useful output is a boundary-and-exchange view, not a detailed internal process. The central system stays one element here. That makes the context clear without introducing the internal tasks or screens that may implement it. Read the diagram back as purpose, boundary, external actors or connected systems, and labeled exchanges.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A context diagram does not expand the system into all its internal activities. It represents the system as one element and shows external entities and exchanges. A connected system is not automatically inside the boundary simply because there is an arrow to it.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the top-level goal is “Prepare an order for dispatch.” Functional decomposition represents that larger goal hierarchically through major tasks and smaller parts.

teaching_blocks.title: Functional Decomposition
teaching_blocks.content: Hierarchical decomposition represents a larger goal as major tasks and breaks those tasks into smaller parts.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Start with the top-level goal, draw its major parts below it, and break each part into relevant subparts. Choose the number of decomposition levels according to the complexity and detail needed.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Draw the goal at the top. In this hypothetical decomposition, its major parts are “Identify order,” “Obtain instructions,” and “Prepare dispatch information.” Beneath Obtain instructions, place “Find current instructions” and “Clarify missing information.” These are illustrative parts of the goal, not a universal dispatch procedure.

Choose the number of levels according to the complexity and detail needed. If the analysis only needs the main parts, stop at that useful level. If a part requires more detail for the purpose, break it into relevant subparts. Do not keep adding levels simply to make every branch the same depth.

The useful output is a hierarchy showing how a larger goal breaks into constituent tasks. It is not necessarily execution order: placing two parts side by side shows that they belong under the same parent, not that they occur simultaneously or in a particular sequence. Keep the parent-child meaning explicit so the learner does not confuse this decomposition with the process flows taught earlier.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A hierarchy of parts is not automatically a sequence of steps. Read lower nodes as subparts of the goal or task above them. The number of levels depends on needed complexity and detail, not an unsupported fixed requirement for every diagram.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a spreadsheet with order amounts in A2:A4 containing 10, 20, and 0, and a factor in B1 containing 0.1. A formula starts with =. To apply the factor to A2, write =A2*$B$1 in C2, then copy it to C3. The relative A2 becomes A3, while the absolute $B$1 stays fixed.

teaching_blocks.title: Cell References and Basic Formulas
teaching_blocks.content: A spreadsheet formula starts with = and may combine cell references, operators, and functions.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A relative reference such as A1 changes when the formula is copied to a different position. An absolute reference such as $A$1 keeps its row and column fixed when copied; $A1 or A$1 fixes just one part. Use =SUM(range) to total values, =AVERAGE(range) for their arithmetic mean, and =COUNT(range) to count numeric cells. Copy a formula containing relative and fixed references and inspect how each reference changes according to the destination. AVERAGE ignores empty cells and text in a referenced range but includes cells containing zero.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
A relative reference such as A1 changes with the copied position. $A$1 fixes both row and column; $A1 fixes only the column, and A$1 fixes only the row. For example, copying a formula from C2 to D3 shifts a relative A1 to B2, keeps $A$1 unchanged, shifts $A1 to $A2, and shifts A$1 to B$1. Inspect the destination formula instead of assuming every reference moves identically.

For the sample amounts, =SUM(A2:A4) returns 30, =AVERAGE(A2:A4) returns 10, and =COUNT(A2:A4) returns 3 because all three cells are numeric. AVERAGE includes zero. If A4 were empty rather than zero, the average of the referenced numbers would be 15, not 10; text and empty cells are ignored in that range calculation.

The practical skill is reading both the calculation and the reference behavior. Fixed references preserve an intended shared input while relative references move to the corresponding source cell when copied.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A dollar sign fixes the part it precedes, not always the whole reference. Also, zero and an empty cell do not have the same effect on AVERAGE: zero is included, while empty cells and text in the referenced range are ignored.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a worksheet has columns Branch and Amount, with North amounts 40 and 60 and South amount 30. A PivotTable can calculate, summarize, and analyze those rows to reveal comparisons rather than displaying only the original records.

teaching_blocks.title: Pivot Tables
teaching_blocks.content: A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK. To add a field to the PivotTable, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; selected fields are added to their default areas, with non-numeric fields added to Rows and numeric fields added to Values, and a field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there. Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable; Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable; Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable; Values area fields are shown as summarized numeric values in the PivotTable.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Select the source data cells, choose Insert > PivotTable, select where to place the report, and choose OK. In the PivotTable Fields pane, check Branch and Amount. The nonnumeric Branch field is added to Rows by default, and the numeric Amount field to Values. Fields can be moved by dragging them to the desired area.

Read the areas deliberately. Rows creates row labels on the left, Columns creates column labels at the top, Values displays summarized numeric values, and Filters provides report filters above the PivotTable. In this hypothetical report, using Branch in Rows and Amount summarized by a total in Values gives North 100 and South 30. That illustrates the intended summary; inspect the numeric summary rather than assuming every possible source field produces the same calculation.

The useful output is a summarized view built from field placement. Moving a field changes its role in the report, so explain the placement in business terms: Branch defines the comparison groups and Amount provides the numeric summary.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Checking a field uses its default placement; that placement is not a permanent rule. Drag fields to the area serving the question. Rows, Columns, Filters, and Values are different roles, and a numeric summary should not be mistaken for an original record.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a customer list with identifiers 101 and 102 in A2:A3 and names North Stores and South Stores in B2:B3. D2 contains the identifier 102. A lookup retrieves the value associated with a matching key.

teaching_blocks.title: Lookup Functions
teaching_blocks.content: A lookup retrieves a value associated with a matching key.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use =XLOOKUP(key, lookup_range, return_range) to find a key and return the corresponding value; exact match is the default. Use =VLOOKUP(key, table_range, column_number, FALSE) for an exact match in the first column and a return value from the specified column to its right. If VLOOKUP’s final argument is omitted or TRUE, it uses approximate matching and expects the first column sorted. Use =INDEX(return_range, MATCH(key, lookup_range, 0)) to return the value at the exact key’s position.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write =XLOOKUP(D2,A2:A3,B2:B3) to return South Stores. Exact match is the default. With the same two-column list, =VLOOKUP(D2,A2:B3,2,FALSE) also returns South Stores: it finds an exact key in the first column and returns column 2 to its right.

Do not omit FALSE casually in this exact-key example. If VLOOKUP’s final argument is omitted or TRUE, it uses approximate matching and expects the first column sorted. That is a different lookup mode, not merely shorter spelling for the exact request.

Another exact form is =INDEX(B2:B3,MATCH(D2,A2:A3,0)). MATCH with 0 finds the exact key’s position, and INDEX returns the value at that position from the return range. In the sample, the key is second and the returned name is South Stores.

The useful BA task is joining a needed business label to a known key through the lookup ranges. Keep the ranges aligned in the example so the matching position corresponds to the intended returned value.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: VLOOKUP’s omitted final argument is not exact matching. For the supported exact pattern, use FALSE; approximate matching expects a sorted first column. XLOOKUP’s exact default and MATCH’s 0 also need to be read as part of the chosen lookup form.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a spreadsheet labels order amounts using a hypothetical policy: amounts above 100 are High, amounts above 50 but not above 100 are Medium, and the rest are Low. A2 contains the amount to classify.

teaching_blocks.title: Conditional Logic and Formulas
teaching_blocks.content: IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two results according to the test.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use =IF(test1, result1, IF(test2, result2, result3)) to express three ordered alternatives. IFS(test1, result1, test2, result2, ...) returns the result for the first true condition. A final TRUE condition in IFS supplies a default result; without a true condition, IFS returns #N/A.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For a two-way decision, =IF(A2>100,"High","Other") returns High when the test is true and Other when it is false. For three ordered alternatives, use =IF(A2>100,"High",IF(A2>50,"Medium","Low")). The second test is reached only through the false alternative of the first.

The same policy can be written =IFS(A2>100,"High",A2>50,"Medium",TRUE,"Low"). IFS returns the result associated with the first true condition; the final TRUE supplies a default. With amounts 120, 75, and 40, the results are High, Medium, and Low. Exactly 100 is Medium and exactly 50 is Low because these tests use >, not an inclusive comparison.

If the IFS expression contains only the two amount tests and neither is true, it returns #N/A. The final TRUE avoids that no-true-condition case by providing the default. The useful skill is tracing ordered tests rather than assuming the formula evaluates all matching labels and combines them.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: In IFS, the first true condition wins. Putting A2>50 before A2>100 would classify 120 as Medium in this policy. A final TRUE supplies a default; without any true condition, IFS returns #N/A rather than an invented blank or Low label.

teaching_notes: Trace boundaries and first-true ordering; no unintroduced AND/OR syntax.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a worksheet with Branch in A1, TotalAmount in B1, and rows North 100 and South 30. The question is a category comparison, so a bar chart fits. A different sheet of amounts by month would support a line chart for a trend over time.

teaching_blocks.title: Data Visualization in Spreadsheets
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the visualization according to the question: bars compare categories and lines show trends over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it

Check the source range and plotted series in the chart task pane, correcting series names or ranges as needed, then use Format to check the chart title, axis titles, and displayed data labels.

teaching_blocks.content:

teaching_blocks.content: A chart type should fit the question, not merely look attractive. Bars support category comparisons and lines support trends over time. Also inspect the plotted source and field placement; a clear title cannot fix a chart using the wrong range.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose an operations manager asks, “Which branch has the largest total order amount in this extract?” Clarify that the desired analysis is a branch-level total, not average order amount or a count of orders.

teaching_blocks.title: Ad Hoc Business Reporting
teaching_blocks.content: Start by clarifying the business outcome or question the analysis should address.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: A spreadsheet pivot table can summarize source data with fields placed in Rows, Columns, and Values. Present the answer prominently and include enough supporting detail for the audience to understand it. Select a table or range, insert a PivotTable, place grouping fields in Rows and the metric in Values, and select an aggregation that answers the business question.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical source, North amounts are 40 and 60 and South amount is 30. Select the source table or range and insert a PivotTable. teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Planning (BA Involvement)
teaching_blocks.content: Sprint Planning collaboratively establishes the work for the iteration.

teaching_blocks.content: Review important backlog items collaboratively and select work that can be completed within the iteration. Inspect candidate items for clear descriptions and sufficient detail, and refine uncertain items before selection. Selection considers the Developers’ capacity and past performance rather than an externally imposed commitment.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Review important backlog items together. For this hypothetical case, the instruction-display item has clear behavior and acceptance detail, while an amendment item still leaves the intended result unclear. Inspect candidate descriptions and refine uncertain items before selection. Select work that can be completed within the iteration.

Consider Developers' capacity and past performance in selection. A stakeholder’s strong preference does not replace that consideration. The BA can help clarify requirements and questions, while the planning discussion remains collaborative rather than becoming a BA-issued delivery promise.

The useful contribution is transparent candidate work with enough detail for the team to reason about selection. If an item cannot yet be understood, record and resolve the uncertainty instead of silently assuming its scope. teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the BA is helping clarify an instruction-access item while the Product Owner and Developers discuss delivery. Product Owner accountability includes maximizing product value and effective backlog management. Some backlog-management work can be delegated, but that does not transfer the accountability.

teaching_blocks.title: Product Owner and Team Collaboration
teaching_blocks.content: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing product value and effective backlog management.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The Product Owner may delegate backlog-management work but remains accountable for it. Clarify backlog items collaboratively while respecting the Product Owner’s ordering accountability and the Developers’ delivery decisions.

teaching_blocks.content:
In this hypothetical collaboration, the BA drafts clearer item wording and brings stakeholder questions to the group. The Product Owner remains accountable for ordering. Developers size the work and decide how selected work will be performed. The BA’s useful contribution is clarification that helps these decisions, not taking them over.

If the BA updates backlog detail under delegated work, distinguish doing that task from becoming accountable for product value and backlog management.

Clear descriptions support collaboration, but they should not be presented as authority to impose order, size, or implementation on the people accountable for those decisions.

teaching_blocks.content: Delegating backlog-management work does not transfer the Product Owner’s accountability. Nor does preparing requirements make the BA responsible for sizing or deciding how selected work is performed. Collaborate on clarity while respecting ordering and delivery boundaries.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Review (BA Involvement)
teaching_blocks.content: The Sprint Review inspects the outcome with stakeholders and determines future adaptations; it is a working session rather than just a presentation.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Acceptance criteria provide the story-specific conditions used to judge whether delivered behavior satisfies the need. Compare the demonstrated behavior with those conditions and discuss differences with the stakeholders.

teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical story, acceptance conditions say that selecting an existing order displays current instructions and an unknown identifier displays a not-found result. Compare the demonstrated behavior with those story-specific conditions. teaching_blocks.content: A presentation of features alone does not capture the review’s working-session purpose. Compare behavior with the story’s acceptance conditions and discuss differences with stakeholders. A convincing demonstration is not evidence that every specified condition was met.
