teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the team completed an iteration but spent significant effort clarifying instruction wording late in the work. The retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness; it is not another stakeholder presentation of the product outcome.

teaching_blocks.title: Sprint Retrospective (BA Involvement)
teaching_blocks.content: The Sprint Retrospective plans ways to improve quality and effectiveness.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how they were or were not solved, considering interactions, processes, and tools. Identify a concrete change that would improve effectiveness and arrange to address the most helpful improvements promptly.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Review what went well, what problems occurred, and how those problems were or were not solved. In this hypothetical discussion, clear customer examples worked well, while late uncertainty about “current instructions” interrupted work. Consider interactions, processes, and tools rather than treating the issue as only one person’s performance.

Identify a concrete change. The team might agree to clarify instruction examples during refinement and arrange to address that helpful improvement promptly. That is an example action chosen for this situation, not a mandatory retrospective technique.

The useful output is a specific improvement the team intends to address, grounded in its review. A record saying only “communicate better” leaves the change unclear. Keep the discussion connected to what happened and what can improve effectiveness, including whether earlier problems were actually solved. The focus is learning about the team’s way of working, not inventing a new product requirement simply because the team has held a meeting.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A retrospective is not just a list of complaints or a repeat of the Sprint Review. It examines quality and effectiveness and leads toward concrete improvements. Naming a problem without identifying a helpful change does not complete that purpose.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Avoid unsupported retrospective ceremonies or mandatory voting methods.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine the problem statement is “Dispatch preparation is delayed by clarification calls.” Ask why those calls occurred. In this hypothetical causal chain, staff could not find current instructions. Ask why that happened: amended instructions remained in a separate record. Ask why they remained separate: the handoff did not identify where the current instruction record should be updated.

teaching_blocks.title: Five Whys
teaching_blocks.content: Five Whys traces a problem’s cause by repeatedly asking why the previous explanation occurred.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write the problem, ask why it happened, record the answer, and ask why that answer happened to extend the causal chain. Five is a guide rather than a required stopping point; use the chain to reach an underlying cause rather than restating the symptom.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Write each answer and use it as the starting point for the next why question. The chain moves from the stated problem toward an underlying cause instead of repeatedly renaming “dispatch delay.” These answers are assumptions provided for the exercise, not a factual diagnosis of a real team’s process.

Five is a guide, not a required stopping point. Do not invent a fifth explanation merely to reach the technique’s name, and do not stop automatically at five if the chain has not reached an underlying cause. Keep the successive explanation visible so a reader can follow how the cause of the previous explanation is being examined.

The useful output is a recorded causal chain tied to the original problem. The technique is not a guarantee that the first plausible answer is the true cause. Repeated why questions should extend the underlying explanation rather than restate the symptom.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: “Why?” followed by the same symptom in different words does not extend the causal chain. Five is not a compulsory count. Avoid manufacturing answers to fill five lines or treating the technique’s name as proof that the fifth answer must be the root cause.

video_need.reason: A drawn question-and-answer chain can show how each why extends the previous explanation.

teaching_notes: All sample causal answers are hypothetical; do not present guesses as verified real causes.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the specific problem is “Orders wait for instruction clarification before dispatch.” A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes for analysis rather than declaring every proposed cause proven.

teaching_blocks.title: Fishbone Diagram
teaching_blocks.content: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes of a problem to support root cause analysis.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Write a specific problem statement, select cause categories appropriate to the problem, and brainstorm potential causes with the team. Place each proposed cause under its category branch to expose patterns; then analyze the proposed causes and agree actions addressing the root cause.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical team discussion, select categories suited to the problem, such as information, handoffs, and tools. Write the problem statement and brainstorm potential causes. Place “amendments stored separately” under information, “unclear update responsibility” under handoffs, and “difficult instruction lookup” under tools. These category names and causes are example choices, not a mandatory universal set.

Use the branches to expose patterns in the proposed causes. Then analyze them and agree actions addressing the root cause. Do not jump from a busy branch to a causal conclusion without that analysis. The diagram’s organizational role helps the team see possibilities; the later analysis is what examines them.

The useful output is a structured cause discussion connected to a specific problem, followed by analyzed causes and agreed actions. A vague problem such as “everything is slow” gives the branches less focus than a concrete statement about waiting for clarification. Keep potential causes explicitly potential until they have been analyzed rather than labeling the diagram a proof of cause.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Putting a cause on a branch does not verify it. A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes, which still need analysis before actions address the root cause. The categories should suit the problem, not be treated as a fixed set every business must use.

video_need.reason: Drawing category branches and placing proposed causes makes organization and later analysis distinct.

teaching_notes: Do not add mandatory cause-category lists or infer cause from number of suggestions.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a team has a shared Definition of Done for an increment. In this hypothetical standard, required quality measures include passing the agreed checks and completing the agreed review. The exact checks are invented for the exercise; the shared standard must be at least as rigorous as any applicable organizational standard.

teaching_blocks.title: Definition of Done
teaching_blocks.content: The Definition of Done describes the state of an increment when it meets the required quality measures.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: The Scrum Team follows a shared Definition of Done, at least as rigorous as any organizational standard. An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review. Check the completed work against the defined quality criteria and identify any unmet criterion before calling it done. Story acceptance criteria specify completion conditions for that particular story rather than replacing the shared quality standard.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Before calling work done, check it against every defined quality criterion and identify unmet criteria. If one required review remains incomplete, the item does not meet the Definition of Done. Under the stated Scrum rule, an item that does not meet it cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review.

Now compare that with a story’s acceptance condition, such as “Selecting an existing order displays current instructions.” The condition specifies completion for this particular story. Even if the behavior satisfies that condition, it does not replace the shared quality standard. The learner needs to distinguish story-specific behavior from the state required of the increment.

The useful output is a clear check against the shared standard, not a subjective declaration that the work looks finished. Keep unmet criteria visible and do not quietly lower the standard to match what was completed. The BA can help clarify story conditions while the Scrum Team follows the shared Definition of Done.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Passing a story’s acceptance criteria does not replace the shared Definition of Done. An item with an unmet required quality criterion cannot be labeled done, released, or presented at Sprint Review under the Definition of Done rule. Do not reinterpret that as merely optional reporting guidance.

video_need.reason: The distinction and the worked business example can be understood from prose; one simple annotated visual is sufficient and a motion demonstration would mostly repeat the text.

teaching_notes: Preserve the release/review restriction and organizational-standard floor explicitly.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a BI model needs to report order amounts by customer and branch. A star schema separates the observations or events from tables that describe business entities.

teaching_blocks.title: Star Schema / Dimensional Modeling for BI
teaching_blocks.content: A star schema separates tables describing business entities from tables storing observations or events.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Dimension tables describe entities and their attributes; their key columns identify rows. Fact tables store observations or events with dimension keys and often numeric measures. Choose the fact table’s grain so its rows describe a consistent level of detail. Connect dimension tables to the central fact table through one-to-many relationships using the dimension’s unique key.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical model, choose the fact grain as one row per order. OrderFact stores order observations, dimension keys, and a numeric amount. CustomerDim and BranchDim describe their entities and attributes, with unique key columns identifying their rows. Connect those dimensions to the central fact table using one-to-many relationships through each dimension’s unique key.

The grain decision keeps the fact rows at a consistent level of detail. Do not mix one row per order with one row per branch-month total in that same example fact table and then describe all rows as equivalent observations. The dimension tables provide descriptive information, while the fact table holds the chosen observations or events and often numeric measures.

The useful mental model is a central fact table surrounded by descriptive dimensions. Keys connect an observation to the relevant descriptions. The example uses numeric Amount; fact tables often have numeric measures, but their fields reflect the observations or events being modeled.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A fact table and a dimension table are not interchangeable because both contain columns. Dimensions describe entities; facts store observations or events at a consistent grain. Mixing detail levels in the example would defeat that grain decision.

video_need.reason: Arranging dimensions around a fact table and highlighting a consistent row grain makes the star structure clear.

teaching_notes: Preserve “often” for numeric measures; do not add unsupported dimensional modeling types.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a Power BI model with CustomerDim and OrderFact. A visual uses customer descriptions and order amounts, so the model relationship needs to propagate filters between related tables.

teaching_blocks.title: Data Model Relationships in BI Tools
teaching_blocks.content: Model relationships propagate filters between related tables so a visual can use fields from multiple tables.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use Modeling > Manage relationships > New and choose the two tables and their matching columns. Set cardinality according to the uniqueness of values on each side and check the active relationship setting. Choose cross-filter direction deliberately: Single propagates filters in one direction and Both allows propagation in both directions.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Use Modeling > Manage relationships > New and choose the two tables and matching columns. For this hypothetical data, CustomerDim.CustomerID is unique and OrderFact.CustomerID repeats across orders, so set cardinality according to that uniqueness and check the active relationship setting.

Choose cross-filter direction deliberately. Single propagates filters in one direction; Both allows propagation in both directions. These are different choices, not an instruction to select Both whenever a report has more than one table. The direction must be considered for the intended filter behavior.

The useful output is a relationship whose matching columns, cardinality, active setting, and filtering direction are understood. If a report combines fields from both tables, explain how the relationship enables filters to reach related data rather than assuming that similar column names are enough. The example stops at the supported relationship settings and does not invent automatic conflict resolution or a universal recommendation for every model.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A relationship is not just a line for display: it propagates filters. Also, Both is not automatically the best setting; it permits two-way propagation and should be chosen deliberately. Check uniqueness and the active setting rather than assuming them.

video_need.reason: Creating a relationship and examining cardinality, active state, and filter direction benefits from tool demonstration.

teaching_notes: No unsupported defaults or claims that bidirectional filtering is universally preferred.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose stakeholders need a Power BI page answering “How do order amounts compare across branches?” A report page contains visuals communicating model information. A service dashboard is a separate collection of tiles, so do not use those names as if they described the same artifact.

teaching_blocks.title: Power BI Dashboard Design
teaching_blocks.content: A Power BI report page contains visuals that communicate information from the model; a service dashboard is a separate collection of tiles.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: In report view, choose fields from the Data pane and a visual type from Visualizations to add a visual to the canvas. Arrange important information prominently and keep the page focused on the audience’s question. Choose comparisons and trends appropriate to the need, avoid clutter, and keep display choices consistent.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
In report view, select fields from the Data pane and a visual type from Visualizations to add a visual to the canvas. For this hypothetical page, use Branch and Amount for the requested comparison. Arrange the most important information prominently and keep the page focused on that audience question.

Choose comparisons or trends appropriate to the need, avoid clutter, and use consistent display choices. A second visual should have a clear role in answering the question instead of being added only because another chart is available. The example does not prescribe a universal number of visuals.

The useful output here is a focused report page, not a service dashboard created by renaming the canvas. The business question guides field choice and arrangement, while the tool actions explain how a beginner places a visual.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A Power BI report page and a service dashboard are distinct. Selecting visuals on the report canvas does not by itself create a dashboard collection of tiles. Also, more visuals do not automatically improve the answer; keep the page focused and consistent.

video_need.reason: Selecting fields and visual types and arranging the report canvas is a concrete tool workflow.

teaching_notes: Explicitly distinguish report page from service dashboard; do not add pinning commands absent from the brief.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a Tableau dashboard for comparing order amounts across branches. First build a worksheet view suitable for that comparison. Drag the category dimension Branch to Rows and numeric measure Amount to Columns, or reverse those placements, and use Bar as the mark type. These placements create the category/value bar view for the example.

teaching_blocks.title: Tableau Dashboard Design
teaching_blocks.content: A Tableau dashboard combines views from worksheets in one place.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Build a worksheet bar chart by dragging a category dimension to Rows and a numeric measure to Columns (or vice versa), using Bar as the mark type; these field placements create the category/value view that can be placed on the dashboard. Select New Dashboard and drag sheets from the dashboard pane onto the canvas. Choose a dashboard size suited to how the audience will view it, and arrange the most important view prominently. Limit the number of views to keep the dashboard focused and readable.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Select New Dashboard and drag the worksheet from the dashboard pane onto the canvas. A Tableau dashboard combines worksheet views in one place; it is not the same artifact as a single worksheet. Choose a dashboard size suited to how the audience will view it, then arrange the most important view prominently.

Limit the views so the dashboard remains focused and readable. If another worksheet adds a useful perspective, give it a clear role. Do not add every worksheet simply because it exists. The particular layout and size are decisions for the audience, not mandatory measurements in this concept.

The useful output is a dashboard built from appropriate worksheet views, with the core comparison visible. The workflow makes both stages explicit: create the category/value worksheet and then place it on the dashboard. A beginner should not be expected to already know how the first chart comes into existence.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A dashboard combines worksheet views; creating a worksheet is not the same as creating the dashboard. Conversely, opening New Dashboard does not create a category/value chart until an appropriate worksheet view is available and placed there.

video_need.reason: Creating the worksheet bar chart and then dragging it onto a new dashboard shows both tool stages.

teaching_notes: Include worksheet bar-chart construction; no invented dashboard size or worksheet count.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose a stakeholder dashboard needs to compare branch amounts and show their change over time. Use bars for the category comparison and lines for the time trend. Choose each visual according to the question it serves.

teaching_blocks.title: Visual Design Principles for Dashboards
teaching_blocks.content: Use chart types that fit the question: bars support category comparisons and lines support trends over time.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Place important information where readers are likely to notice it and keep the layout focused. Use color consistently and avoid unnecessary variety or decoration that distracts from the data. Reduce unnecessary views and labels so the intended comparison remains readable.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Place the most important information where readers are likely to notice it and keep the layout focused. In this hypothetical page, the branch comparison is the primary question, so give it prominence rather than burying it beneath unrelated views. The exact position is a layout choice for the example, not a universal pixel rule.

Use color consistently and avoid unnecessary variation or decoration that distracts from the data. Reduce unnecessary views and labels so the intended comparison stays readable. Removing a distracting label does not mean removing information needed to interpret the chart; the aim is a clear comparison.

The useful output is a visual design whose chart type, prominence, color, and level of detail support the stakeholder question. Styling choices should not replace the answer. A dashboard full of differently colored charts can still fail to communicate which comparison matters if the layout and views do not remain focused.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Decoration is not automatically information. Unnecessary color variety, views, and labels can distract from the intended comparison. But reducing clutter is not a license to remove needed context; preserve readability while keeping important information noticeable.

video_need.reason: A simple annotated layout comparison is sufficient to show focus, chart choice, and consistent color.

teaching_notes: No unsupported color prescriptions, fixed layout rules, or chart count limits.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Imagine a Power BI Desktop report is ready for the operations audience. Use Home > Publish and choose the destination workspace in the Power BI service. Publishing is the named step for sending the Desktop report to that workspace; the audience still needs appropriate sharing and access.

teaching_blocks.title: Stakeholder-Facing Report Delivery
teaching_blocks.content: Publish a Desktop report with Home > Publish and choose a destination workspace in the Power BI service.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Select Share for a report or dashboard and specify recipients or an appropriate sharing link. Choose whether recipients can reshare or build on the underlying data and grant only the permissions the audience needs. Sharing and access depend on license and capacity; sharing generally requires Pro or PPU, and free recipients require eligible Premium or Fabric capacity.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
Select Share for the report or dashboard and specify recipients or an appropriate sharing link. Choose whether recipients can reshare or build on the underlying data, granting only the permissions the audience needs. In this hypothetical case, readers need to consume the report, so do not enable broader permissions merely because the options are available.

Check licensing and capacity conditions. Sharing generally requires Pro or PPU, and free recipients require eligible Premium or Fabric capacity. These are qualified access conditions, not a promise that any recipient with a link can open every shared artifact.

The useful output is a published report shared to its intended audience with considered permissions and access prerequisites. Keep workspace selection, recipient or link selection, permission choices, and license/capacity checks distinct. A successful publish does not establish that each intended recipient satisfies the sharing conditions.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A link does not by itself override licensing or capacity requirements. Publishing and sharing also address different steps. Grant reshare or build permissions only when needed, and preserve “generally” in the license statement rather than turning it into an unconditional universal rule.

video_need.reason: Publish, Share, permissions, and access checks are best understood through the corresponding interface actions.

teaching_notes: Avoid exhaustive licensing advice; retain stated Pro/PPU and eligible capacity qualifications.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose OrderFact contains Amount and Quantity. A measure can total Amount while responding to current report filters. Use Modeling > New measure and enter:
TotalAmount = SUM(OrderFact[Amount])
With hypothetical North amounts 40 and 60 and South amount 30, the unfiltered total is 130 and the North-filtered total is 100.

teaching_blocks.title: Power BI Measures and Calculated Columns (DAX)
teaching_blocks.content: A DAX measure calculates a result that changes with the current report filtering and selection context.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Use Modeling > New measure and enter MeasureName = SUM(TableName[NumericColumn]) to define a basic total that responds to report context. A calculated column uses a DAX expression to calculate a value for each row rather than the measure’s report-context result. Use New Column and write column_name = expression; the formula is applied across the table’s rows. In standard Import mode, calculated-column values are materialized and refreshed when the underlying data is refreshed. For a classic date-column time-intelligence calculation, use a marked date table whose Date or date/time column contains unique, nonblank dates without gaps and spans full years, including the periods being compared. Relate the date table to the metric table’s relevant date column with an active relationship so that report filters on the date table propagate to the metric’s rows. Evaluate the base total measure in the current date filter context and obtain its corresponding prior-year value with PriorYear = CALCULATE([MeasureName], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])), which evaluates that measure with the dates shifted one year back. Compute year-over-year growth with Growth = DIVIDE([MeasureName] - [PriorYear], [PriorYear]) and format it as a percentage; without an alternate result, DIVIDE returns BLANK when the prior-year denominator is zero or blank.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
A calculated column instead evaluates an expression for each row. Use New Column and enter:
DoubleQuantity = OrderFact[Quantity] * 2
Rows with quantities 2 and 3 receive 4 and 6. In standard Import mode these values are materialized and refreshed when underlying data is refreshed; do not describe them as the same report-context calculation as a measure.

For the classic date-column prior-year pattern, first use a marked date table with unique, nonblank, gap-free dates spanning full years and the compared periods. Relate it actively to the fact table’s relevant date column so date filters propagate. Then define:
PriorYear = CALCULATE([TotalAmount], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
This evaluates the base measure with dates shifted one year back. Define growth with:
Growth = DIVIDE([TotalAmount] - [PriorYear], [PriorYear])
and format it as a percentage.

For an example current total of 120 and corresponding prior-year total of 100, growth is (120 − 100) / 100 = 20%. Without an alternate result, DIVIDE returns BLANK when the denominator is zero or blank. Keep the date prerequisites visible: the formula is not a substitute for the marked date table and active relationship required by this pattern.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Measures and calculated columns are not two names for the same evaluation. The measure responds to report context; the column calculates each row and, in standard Import mode, materializes values on refresh. For growth, divide the difference by prior year—not current year—and do not omit the date-table prerequisites.

video_need.reason: Creating measures and columns, changing filters, and checking date-model prerequisites makes evaluation context and time comparison visible.

teaching_notes: Keep Import-mode qualification and classic date-column prerequisites; avoid unintroduced DAX functions.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content:
Imagine a Tableau source with Sales and Discount. A calculated field derives new data from existing fields without changing the original source. Use Analysis > Create Calculated Field, name the field Discount Ratio, enter the expression, and select OK:
IIF([Sales] !=0, [Discount]/[Sales],0)

teaching_blocks.title: Tableau Calculated Fields
teaching_blocks.content: A Tableau calculated field derives new data from existing fields without changing the original source.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Choose Analysis > Create Calculated Field, name the field, enter an expression, and select OK. The Discount Ratio calculation is IIF([Sales] !=0, [Discount]/[Sales],0): it returns Discount divided by Sales when Sales is nonzero, and zero otherwise. A basic calculation may operate at the row level or at the visualization’s aggregate level, depending on its expression. Numeric calculated fields can be summed automatically when added to a view; change the aggregation if the intended metric requires a different one.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For hypothetical rows with Sales 100 and Discount 10, and Sales 0 and Discount 0, the calculated values are 0.1 and 0. The expression returns Discount divided by Sales when Sales is nonzero, and zero otherwise. It does not establish that a missing value behaves like zero; this example uses known numeric values only.

A basic calculation can operate at row level or at the visualization’s aggregate level, depending on the expression. Numeric calculated fields can be summed automatically when added to a view, so inspect whether that aggregation fits the intended metric. With rows having ratios 0.1 and 0.2, summing the row ratios gives 0.3; do not label that automatically as the intended business discount metric.

The useful output is a calculated field with an understood expression and a deliberate view aggregation. Creating the field and deciding how to summarize it are separate analytical concerns.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: A calculated field does not modify the original source. Also, a numeric field’s automatic sum is not proof that sum is the appropriate metric. Inspect the expression’s level and choose aggregation for the business question rather than blindly accepting the initial view.

video_need.reason: Creating the field and checking how its numeric values aggregate in a view benefits from a tool demonstration.

teaching_notes: No unsupported NULL or divide-by-zero claims beyond the IIF result; avoid new aggregation syntax.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.

teaching_blocks.content: Suppose operations and sales each need a report using the same total-order-amount calculation. A Power BI semantic model contains data-model logic that reports can use. Reusing one published model avoids having each report create separate data and calculation definitions for this shared need.

teaching_blocks.title: BI Semantic Layer
teaching_blocks.content: A Power BI semantic model contains data-model logic that can be used to build reports.

teaching_blocks.title: How to apply it
teaching_blocks.content: Reports can reuse an existing published semantic model rather than each creating separate data and calculation definitions. Define the shared business calculation as a measure in the common model and use that model for reports that need the same calculation. Connect a new report to the existing shared semantic model; building content on a shared model requires Build permission.

teaching_blocks.title: A business analysis example
teaching_blocks.content:
For this hypothetical arrangement, define the shared business calculation as a measure in the common model. Build both reports from that model when they need the same calculation. One report may focus on branches and another on customers while using the shared calculation definition.

Connect a new report to the existing shared semantic model. Building content on it requires Build permission, so do not assume access to a finished report automatically grants authority to build new content from its model.

The useful mental model is shared data-model logic supporting multiple reports, rather than every report independently recreating the same business calculation. The example does not promise every report will display the same result under different filters; it is the common calculation definition that is reused. Keep the distinction between shared model, report, and required Build permission clear.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep the distinction clear
teaching_blocks.content: Sharing a calculation definition does not mean every differently filtered report displays an identical number. Reports reuse model logic. Also, building new content on the shared model requires Build permission; do not treat mere report access as that permission.

video_need.reason: A model-to-multiple-reports diagram can clarify shared calculations and the separate Build permission requirement.

teaching_notes: Do not invent connection UI steps; distinguish shared definition from filtered result.
Use the supplied hypothetical business situation; do not treat its policies, numbers, or outcomes as universal rules.
